colophon.title: Pa o Kachatbingna Kasa wui Khararchan: The Acts of the Apostles

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 1: Kazingli Kaphan kala Kachatbing (Ascension and Commission)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Theophilus-li kaphung kakhanin: Jesu-na khararchanli ot kasawui maram kaphung-kachungli kaphika thotsai. Awui thikahaiwui saphunga A haringkasa theichithei kachiva thotna athumli thang taracham kachithei Varivarawui kazingramwui tui hosa. Mangan Kathara nithumwui kachungli raranglikha nithum pangmashan phunglikha; kala Jerusalemli, Judea kala Samaria ram kachivali, kala ngalei pammai kashung kachivali Iwui sakhibing salikha. Athumna theishak phashokda Matthiasli rasai, kala aya kachatbing tarakhatli ngasohailsai.
excerpts.translation_en: The former treatise have I made, O Theophilus, of all that Jesus began both to do and teach. To whom also he shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days. But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 2: Pentecost Thangli Mangan Kathara (Day of Pentecost)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Pentecost kumshang phungphatli nithum pam akhangli zikahai pamsai. Kazingwui huchiphung majung katha khara rasai, kala athum pamsahai shim kachivali kapingsai. Kala meiwui malei katha khangayeida athum kachivawui kachungli rasai. Kala athum kachiva Mangan Katharana kapingda ngatei tui khangayei hosa! Peterna ngakarangda hosa: Israel miwung, tui hi ngashonlu: Nazarethwui Jesu hili Varivarana thikahaiwui ngachaili thingkashangsai; chiwui maramli ithum kachiva sakhibing thotsai. Ningzan ngashunlu, kala nithum kachiva Jesu Christawui minli baptisma sayanlu!
excerpts.translation_en: And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues. Then Peter stood up and said, Ye men of Israel, hear these words; This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses. Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 3: Temple Gate wui Pamli Thotkhamatei (Lame Man at the Beautiful Gate)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Peter kala John thangkhamir pung chiko khangamor thangli Templeli zangvangasai. Phaphuk khazat akhat, awui phankahaiwui thotli theisai, aya Templewui Mathan Gate kahowali pamsai; aya Peter kala Johnli theida seisan khamor khanasai. Peterna hosa: Rupa kala sona iwui chungli mathai mana; kha ina phungli nali khamlikha: Nazarethwui Jesu Christawui minli ngakarangda zatlu! Kala ayana awui pangkasho pangda thingkasangsai; chitharan awui phakhur kala pharu pangmashan phungsai! Aya ngachor-da ngakarangsai kala zat-zangsai, Templeli zangda khangachor kala Varivarali mathankashei sasai.
excerpts.translation_en: Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour. And a certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple. Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk. And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength. And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 4: Councilwui Phungli Sakhi Chitheikahai (Before the Sanhedrin)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Athumna Peter kala Johnli ngachaili pamsahai hosa: Khipawui pangmashan kala minli nithumna hi sakha? Peterna Mangan Katharana kapingda hosa: Miwungwui khararbing kala Israelwui Hangvabing, ngatei khipawui chunglikha haring kaphan mathailak mana; maramchilu kazing kaphungli miwungli khami ngatei min khikha mathai mana! Kha athumna Peter kala Johnna ngahanda hosa: Nithumwui tui ngashon-katha Varivarawui tui ngashon-katha khipana mashungkha nithum shanshilu! Maramchilu ithumna theikahai kala ngashokahai tui masasa pamtang mathailak mana.
excerpts.translation_en: And when they had set them in the midst, they asked, By what power, or by what name, have ye done this? Then Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost, said unto them, Ye rulers of the people, and elders of Israel, Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved. But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 5: Stephenwui Pao kala Kashung Thot (The Martyrdom of Stephen)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Stephenna ning-kachang kala pangmashan phungda miwungwui ngachaili theichithei kaphung sasai. Council shimli pambing kachivana ali theida awui mai kazingram kachisowui mai katha theisai. Kha aya Mangan Katharana kapingda kazingli theida Varivarawui mathankashak theisai. Kala athumna lungna chidatli Stephenna khon-kaphung: O Mapao Jesu, iwui mangankhali khaphanlu! Kala aya phakhur phumda kaho: O Mapao, kakhama hi athumwui chungli machonlu! Hi hoda aya thikahaisai. Saulna awui thikahaili ningkachang phungsai.
excerpts.translation_en: And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people. And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel. But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God. And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep. And Saul was consenting unto his death.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 6: Corneliusli Pao Kazang (Conversion of Cornelius)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Caesarea ramli Cornelius kahona Italian cohortwui centurion akhat pamsai. Aya Varivarali kacharan, awui shim kachiva ngasoda, miwungli dori khami kala Varivarali thang kachiva khangamor. Peterna Caesareali rada hosa: Kaphung-kachangli ina theisai Varivarana mi akhatli kaching mei mana; kha ram kachivali Ali kacharan kala mashungkasa chi Awui ningkachang phungsai. Peterna tui hi holikha Mangan Katharana tui ngashonbing kachivawui chungli rasai!
excerpts.translation_en: There was a certain man in Caesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band, A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway. Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him. While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 7: Athens Ramli Paulna Tui Chitheikahai (Paul at the Areopagus)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Paulna Areopagus (Mars Hill) ngachaili ngakarangda hosa: Athens miwung, ina theisai nithum thang kachiva kameo khangamor phungsai; maramchilu ina zatli nithumwui altar akhatli kaphika theisai: MATHIKAHAI VARIVARALI. Nithumna matheila khangamor hili ina chitheikhami! Kazing kala ngalei kala chili leisatha kachiva sakahai Varivara chili kazing kala ngaleiwui Mapaosai, Aya mina sakahai templeli mapam mana; maramchilu Awui chungli ithum haring, zatta, kala pamsai; nithumwui la-kashabingna hokatha: 'Ithumya Awui kachung thotsai.'
excerpts.translation_en: Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

title: History of the Tangkhul Nagas
subject: History, Ethnography, and Customary Institutions
notes: Comprehensive ethnographic and historical treatise by A.S.W. Shimray detailing Makhel origins, the Awunga chieftaincy, and village republics.

front_matter.preface: History of the Tangkhul Nagas by A. S. W. Shimray (Akansha Publishing House, New Delhi, 2001, ISBN 81-87606-04-5). A comprehensive ethnographic, historical, and sociological monograph documenting Tangkhul origin traditions from Makhel, village republic governance under the Awunga and Hangva, agricultural engineering, clan land tenures, ritual warfare, and modern political integration.

chapters.title: Origin Traditions and Migration from Makhel
chapters.summary: Ancient origins at Makhel and Khezhakenoma, the myth of the three brothers, and settlement of the Ukhrul ridge.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul oral literature unequivocally traces ancestral migrations back to Makhel in northern Manipur and contiguous Khezhakenoma. From Makhel, three brothers departed: the eldest became the Meitei of the valley, the middle the Tangkhul of the eastern hills, and the youngest the Northern Naga groups. Hundung and Hunphun represent the dual pivotal chieftaincies from which daughter settlements radiated throughout the Raphei (Northern), Rem (Western), Kharao (Southern), and Khanggo (Eastern) geographical divisions. While standard Tangkhul is based on the dialect of Hunphun, the tribe comprises over one hundred villages.
chapters.english_translation: Tangkhul oral literature unequivocally traces ancestral migrations back to Makhel in northern Manipur and contiguous Khezhakenoma. From Makhel, three brothers departed: the eldest became the Meitei of the valley, the middle the Tangkhul of the eastern hills, and the youngest the Northern Naga groups. Hundung and Hunphun represent the dual pivotal chieftaincies from which daughter settlements radiated throughout the Raphei, Rem, Kharao, and Khanggo geographical divisions. Over one hundred villages maintain distinct idioms.

vocabulary.meaning: sacred ancestral dispersal village of the Naga tribes
eastern border division contiguous to Myanmar

chapters.grammar_notes: Toponyms like 'Raphei' and 'Kharao' function as regional dialect and sociocultural identifiers.

exercises.question: What three brother-groups departed from Makhel in Tangkhul tradition?
Name the four ancient geographical divisions of the Tangkhul hills.

chapters.title: The Village Republic: Awunga and the Hangva Council
chapters.summary: Village sovereignty (Wungram), the hereditary chief (Awunga), the clan elder bench (Hangva), and the Longshim dormitory.
chapters.tangkhul_text: The traditional Tangkhul village was an autonomous republic with defined territorial borders. At the head of each village stood the Awunga (hereditary chief), governing in strict concert with the Hangva (Council of Elders representing all village clans). The Hangva met at the Awunga's courtyard to adjudicate disputes, announce festival schedules, declare seasonal taboos (khamthei), and decide matters of peace or war. Decisions were reached through consensus (ngalung). Integral to village life was the Longshim (youth dormitory system) which served as the civic militia and school of etiquette.
chapters.english_translation: The traditional Tangkhul village was an autonomous republic with defined territorial borders. At the head of each village stood the Awunga (hereditary chief), governing in strict concert with the Hangva (Council of Elders representing all clans). The Hangva met at the chief's courtyard to adjudicate disputes, announce festival schedules, declare seasonal taboos, and decide peace or war. Consensus (ngalung) governed all decisions. The Longshim dormitory trained youth in civic defense and customary etiquette.
chapters.grammar_notes: The compound 'Wungram' joins 'Wung' (indigenous ethnonym) with 'ram' (land / country / territory).

exercises.question: How did the Hangva council reach decisions under customary governance?
Describe the educational and defensive roles of the Longshim dormitory.

chapters.title: Agricultural Regimes: Luingam and Shilmik
chapters.summary: Terrace cultivation (Luingam), swidden farming (Shilmik), irrigation channels (kong-kuir), and the Luira festival.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul subsistence economy was anchored upon wet-rice terrace cultivation (Luingam) and rotational swidden farming (Shilmik). Terraces along mountain slopes required gravity-fed irrigation channels (kong-kuir) maintained collectively by syndicates. The agricultural calendar opened with the Luira Phanit (seed-sowing festival) in February. No villager was permitted to sow until the Awunga performed the sacred first sowing ritual. Harvest was celebrated with Chumpha in December, consecrating newly garnered paddy in village granaries (raizan).
chapters.english_translation: Tangkhul subsistence economy was anchored upon wet-rice terrace cultivation (Luingam) and rotational swidden farming (Shilmik). Terraces along mountain slopes required gravity-fed irrigation channels (kong-kuir) maintained collectively by syndicates. The agricultural year began with Luira Phanit in February with the chief's sacred first sowing, and closed with Chumpha in December, consecrating newly stored grain in family granaries.

vocabulary.meaning: wet-rice terrace cultivation, irrigated terrace field
granary, raised storehouse for harvested paddy

chapters.grammar_notes: Compound root 'luira' combines 'lui' (terrace field) and 'ra' (water / festival rites).

exercises.question: What is the distinction between Luingam and Shilmik cultivation?
Which festivals mark the opening and closing of the Tangkhul farming cycle?

chapters.title: Clan Kinship (Shang) and Land Tenure
chapters.summary: Exogamous patrilineal clans (Shang), inheritance by male primogeniture, and the sacrosanct role of Pukreila peace envoys.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul society is strictly exogamous and patrilineal, organized into clans (shang) and sub-lineages (shimkhor). Marriage within the clan was strictly prohibited as shiman-kaphung. Land tenure was threefold: communal village land, clan land, and family hereditary plots. Ancestral homesteads passed through male primogeniture. When villages entered formal treaties, high-status women born in one village and married into the other acted as Pukreila (peace ambassadors). The person of the Pukreila was sacrosanct; harming an ambassador was regarded as an unforgivable breach invoking divine retribution.
chapters.english_translation: Tangkhul society is strictly exogamous and patrilineal, organized into clans (shang) and sub-lineages (shimkhor). Intra-clan marriage was strictly prohibited. Land tenure comprised communal village land, clan reserves, and family plots. Homesteads passed via male primogeniture. Inter-village treaties were mediated by Pukreila (female peace ambassadors). The person of the Pukreila was sacrosanct, and harming an ambassador invoked severe divine retribution.

vocabulary.meaning: female peace ambassador, sacrosanct treaty envoy
divine retribution, cosmic curse on covenant breakers

chapters.grammar_notes: The feminine suffix '-la' in 'Pukreila' designates an honored woman functioning in ambassadorial capacity.

exercises.question: Explain the diplomatic and moral functions of the Pukreila in Naga warfare.
What are the three categories of land ownership under Tangkhul customary law?

chapters.title: Head-Taking (Rai) and Peacemaking Rituals
chapters.summary: The ritual logic of head-taking, the village skull repository, and the solemn covenant of spear burial.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Head-taking among the Tangkhul was bound to cosmological balance, fertility of crops, and personal valor. It was ritual warfare governed by strict customary boundaries. Heads taken were brought to the village entrance, received with ritual chants, and hung at the sacred village tree (khor-thing) or deposited at the village skull depository. Wars were concluded through the solemn ceremony of spear burial (kachu-kapam) and the consumption of ceremonial pork and rice-beer between combatant Awungas. Broken oaths brought calamity upon future generations.
chapters.english_translation: Head-taking among the Tangkhul was bound to cosmological balance, fertility of crops, and personal valor. It was ritual warfare governed by strict customary boundaries. Heads taken were brought to the village entrance, hung at the sacred village tree (khor-thing) or placed in the skull depository. Wars concluded through the ceremony of spear burial (kachu-kapam) and mutual consumption of ceremonial food by chiefs, sealing eternal oaths.

vocabulary.meaning: sacred village tree, warrior trophy oak
war horn, buffalo horn trumpet sounding alarm or victory

chapters.grammar_notes: Compound verbal noun 'kachu-kapam' pairs 'kachu' (spear) with 'kapam' (planting/burying deeply).

exercises.question: How did Tangkhul warriors conclude peace after warfare?
What cosmological beliefs were associated with head-taking?

chapters.title: Traditional Religion: Kameo, Varivara, and Feasts of Merit
chapters.summary: Cosmological belief in the Supreme God (Varivara), spirits of nature (Kameo), and memorial Feasts of Merit (Maringphat).
chapters.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul cosmology recognized a Supreme Creator God (Varivara) who dwelt in the highest heavens, benevolent and just. Beneath Varivara were regional nature spirits (Kameo) inhabiting sacred groves, cliffs, and peaks. Propitiatory offerings were made by the village priest (Maiba) to appease spirits. Wealthy individuals who accumulated surplus grain and cattle performed progressive Feasts of Merit (Maringphat), feeding the entire village community and allied settlements for multiple days, erecting memorial megaliths (lung-thei), and carving house-fronts with horn-motifs (lengcheng-pakhang).
chapters.english_translation: Tangkhul cosmology recognized a Supreme Creator God (Varivara) who dwelt in the highest heavens, benevolent and just. Beneath Varivara were nature spirits (Kameo) inhabiting sacred groves, cliffs, and peaks, propitiated by the priest (Maiba). Wealthy individuals performed progressive Feasts of Merit (Maringphat), hosting the entire community for multiple days, erecting memorial megaliths (lung-thei), and carving house facades with ceremonial horn motifs.

vocabulary.meaning: Feast of Merit, progressive socioeconomic feast
memorial stone megalith, standing commemorative stone
house-horns, carved gable-planks of feast givers

chapters.grammar_notes: Nominal compound 'lung-thei' combines 'lung' (stone) with stative 'thei' (manifest / conspicuous).

exercises.question: What cultural privileges did a Feast of Merit confer upon a Tangkhul family?
Distinguish between the supreme role of Varivara and localized Kameo spirits.

chapters.title: The Colonial Encounter and Political Awakenings
chapters.summary: Colonial pacification, William Pettigrew's mission school in Ukhrul, and the emergence of modern Naga consciousness.
chapters.tangkhul_text: The arrival of British administration in the late 19th century and the establishment of Rev. William Pettigrew's mission school at Ukhrul in 1896 initiated dramatic socioeconomic transformations. Roman script literacy, modern medical care, and Christianity gradually replaced the head-taking regime. Yet Tangkhul customary laws, land rights, and village identity endured, forming the foundation of modern Naga political consciousness and solidarity in northeast India.
chapters.english_translation: British colonial administration and Rev. William Pettigrew's mission school in 1896 at Ukhrul catalyzed profound transformations. Roman literacy, healthcare, and Christianity gradually replaced the warfare regime. Yet customary laws, ancestral land tenure, and village identity endured, providing the bedrock of modern Naga political solidarity in northeast India.

vocabulary.meaning: elevation and dignity of the Tangkhul homeland
the missionary era, advent of modern education (1896+)

chapters.grammar_notes: Temporal genitive 'Pettigrew-wui thot' marks the pivotal historical turning point in modern Tangkhul historiography.

exercises.question: When did Rev. William Pettigrew establish the first school in Ukhrul?
How did customary land tenure survive colonial and post-colonial governance?

pages.header: Chapter 3: Agricultural Regimes: Luingam and Shilmik (Page 10)
pages.title: Chapter 3: Agricultural Regimes: Luingam and Shilmik
lines: CHAPTER 3: AGRICULTURAL REGIMES: LUINGAM AND SHILMIK
Summary: Terrace cultivation (Luingam), swidden farming (Shilmik), irrigation channels (kong-kuir), and the Luira festival.
Tangkhul subsistence economy was anchored upon wet-rice terrace
cultivation (Luingam) and rotational swidden farming (Shilmik). Terraces
along mountain slopes required gravity-fed irrigation channels (kong-
kuir) maintained collectively by syndicates. The agricultural calendar
opened with the Luira Phanit (seed-sowing festival) in February. No
villager was permitted to sow until the Awunga performed the sacred
first sowing ritual. Harvest was celebrated with Chumpha in December,
consecrating newly garnered paddy in village granaries (raizan).

pages.title: Chapter 5: Head-Taking (Rai) and Peacemaking Rituals
lines: Summary: The ritual logic of head-taking, the village skull repository, and the solemn covenant of spear burial.
Head-taking among the Tangkhul was bound to cosmological balance,
fertility of crops, and personal valor. It was ritual warfare governed
by strict customary boundaries. Heads taken were brought to the village
entrance, received with ritual chants, and hung at the sacred village
tree (khor-thing) or deposited at the village skull depository. Wars
were concluded through the solemn ceremony of spear burial (kachu-kapam)
and the consumption of ceremonial pork and rice-beer between combatant
Awungas. Broken oaths brought calamity upon future generations.

Tangkhul cosmology recognized a Supreme Creator God (Varivara) who dwelt
in the highest heavens, benevolent and just. Beneath Varivara were
nature spirits (Kameo) inhabiting sacred groves, cliffs, and peaks,

pages.tangkhul_content: Tangkhul cosmology recognized a Supreme Creator God (Varivara) who dwelt in the highest heavens, benevolent and just. Beneath Varivara were regional nature spirits (Kameo) inhabiting sacred groves, cliffs, and peaks. Propitiatory offerings were made by the village priest (Maiba) to appease spirits. Wealthy individuals who accumulated surplus grain and cattle performed progressive Feasts of Merit (Maringphat), feeding the entire village community and allied settlements for multiple days, erecting memorial megaliths (lung-thei), and carving house-fronts with horn-motifs (lengcheng-pakhang).

Wealthy individuals performed progressive Feasts of Merit (Maringphat), hosting the entire community for multiple days, erecting memorial megaliths (lung-thei), and carving house facades with ceremonial horn motifs.

pages.header: Chapter 7: The Colonial Encounter and Political Awakenings (Page 19)
pages.title: Chapter 7: The Colonial Encounter and Political Awakenings
lines: CHAPTER 7: THE COLONIAL ENCOUNTER AND POLITICAL AWAKENINGS
Summary: Colonial pacification, William Pettigrew's mission school in Ukhrul, and the emergence of modern Naga consciousness.
The arrival of British administration in the late 19th century and the
establishment of Rev. William Pettigrew's mission school at Ukhrul in
1896 initiated dramatic socioeconomic transformations. Roman script
literacy, modern medical care, and Christianity gradually replaced the
head-taking regime. Yet Tangkhul customary laws, land rights, and
village identity endured, forming the foundation of modern Naga
political consciousness and solidarity in northeast India.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 1: Origin Traditions and Migration from Makhel
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul oral literature unequivocally traces ancestral migrations back to Makhel in northern Manipur and contiguous Khezhakenoma. From Makhel, three brothers departed: the eldest became the Meitei of the valley, the middle the Tangkhul of the eastern hills, and the youngest the Northern Naga groups. Hundung and Hunphun represent the dual pivotal chieftaincies from which daughter settlements radiated throughout the Raphei (Northern), Rem (Western), Kharao (Southern), and Khanggo (Eastern) geographical divisions. While standard Tangkhul is based on the dialect of Hunphun, the tribe comprises over one hundred villages.
excerpts.translation_en: Tangkhul oral literature unequivocally traces ancestral migrations back to Makhel in northern Manipur and contiguous Khezhakenoma. From Makhel, three brothers departed: the eldest became the Meitei of the valley, the middle the Tangkhul of the eastern hills, and the youngest the Northern Naga groups. Hundung and Hunphun represent the dual pivotal chieftaincies from which daughter settlements radiated throughout the Raphei, Rem, Kharao, and Khanggo geographical divisions. Over one hundred villages maintain distinct idioms.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 2: The Village Republic: Awunga and the Hangva Council
excerpts.tangkhul_text: The traditional Tangkhul village was an autonomous republic with defined territorial borders. At the head of each village stood the Awunga (hereditary chief), governing in strict concert with the Hangva (Council of Elders representing all village clans). The Hangva met at the Awunga's courtyard to adjudicate disputes, announce festival schedules, declare seasonal taboos (khamthei), and decide matters of peace or war. Decisions were reached through consensus (ngalung). Integral to village life was the Longshim (youth dormitory system) which served as the civic militia and school of etiquette.
excerpts.translation_en: The traditional Tangkhul village was an autonomous republic with defined territorial borders. At the head of each village stood the Awunga (hereditary chief), governing in strict concert with the Hangva (Council of Elders representing all clans). The Hangva met at the chief's courtyard to adjudicate disputes, announce festival schedules, declare seasonal taboos, and decide peace or war. Consensus (ngalung) governed all decisions. The Longshim dormitory trained youth in civic defense and customary etiquette.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 3: Agricultural Regimes: Luingam and Shilmik
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul subsistence economy was anchored upon wet-rice terrace cultivation (Luingam) and rotational swidden farming (Shilmik). Terraces along mountain slopes required gravity-fed irrigation channels (kong-kuir) maintained collectively by syndicates. The agricultural calendar opened with the Luira Phanit (seed-sowing festival) in February. No villager was permitted to sow until the Awunga performed the sacred first sowing ritual. Harvest was celebrated with Chumpha in December, consecrating newly garnered paddy in village granaries (raizan).
excerpts.translation_en: Tangkhul subsistence economy was anchored upon wet-rice terrace cultivation (Luingam) and rotational swidden farming (Shilmik). Terraces along mountain slopes required gravity-fed irrigation channels (kong-kuir) maintained collectively by syndicates. The agricultural year began with Luira Phanit in February with the chief's sacred first sowing, and closed with Chumpha in December, consecrating newly stored grain in family granaries.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 4: Clan Kinship (Shang) and Land Tenure
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul society is strictly exogamous and patrilineal, organized into clans (shang) and sub-lineages (shimkhor). Marriage within the clan was strictly prohibited as shiman-kaphung. Land tenure was threefold: communal village land, clan land, and family hereditary plots. Ancestral homesteads passed through male primogeniture. When villages entered formal treaties, high-status women born in one village and married into the other acted as Pukreila (peace ambassadors). The person of the Pukreila was sacrosanct; harming an ambassador was regarded as an unforgivable breach invoking divine retribution.
excerpts.translation_en: Tangkhul society is strictly exogamous and patrilineal, organized into clans (shang) and sub-lineages (shimkhor). Intra-clan marriage was strictly prohibited. Land tenure comprised communal village land, clan reserves, and family plots. Homesteads passed via male primogeniture. Inter-village treaties were mediated by Pukreila (female peace ambassadors). The person of the Pukreila was sacrosanct, and harming an ambassador invoked severe divine retribution.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 5: Head-Taking (Rai) and Peacemaking Rituals
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Head-taking among the Tangkhul was bound to cosmological balance, fertility of crops, and personal valor. It was ritual warfare governed by strict customary boundaries. Heads taken were brought to the village entrance, received with ritual chants, and hung at the sacred village tree (khor-thing) or deposited at the village skull depository. Wars were concluded through the solemn ceremony of spear burial (kachu-kapam) and the consumption of ceremonial pork and rice-beer between combatant Awungas. Broken oaths brought calamity upon future generations.
excerpts.translation_en: Head-taking among the Tangkhul was bound to cosmological balance, fertility of crops, and personal valor. It was ritual warfare governed by strict customary boundaries. Heads taken were brought to the village entrance, hung at the sacred village tree (khor-thing) or placed in the skull depository. Wars concluded through the ceremony of spear burial (kachu-kapam) and mutual consumption of ceremonial food by chiefs, sealing eternal oaths.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 6: Traditional Religion: Kameo, Varivara, and Feasts of Merit
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Tangkhul cosmology recognized a Supreme Creator God (Varivara) who dwelt in the highest heavens, benevolent and just. Beneath Varivara were regional nature spirits (Kameo) inhabiting sacred groves, cliffs, and peaks. Propitiatory offerings were made by the village priest (Maiba) to appease spirits. Wealthy individuals who accumulated surplus grain and cattle performed progressive Feasts of Merit (Maringphat), feeding the entire village community and allied settlements for multiple days, erecting memorial megaliths (lung-thei), and carving house-fronts with horn-motifs (lengcheng-pakhang).
excerpts.translation_en: Tangkhul cosmology recognized a Supreme Creator God (Varivara) who dwelt in the highest heavens, benevolent and just. Beneath Varivara were nature spirits (Kameo) inhabiting sacred groves, cliffs, and peaks, propitiated by the priest (Maiba). Wealthy individuals performed progressive Feasts of Merit (Maringphat), hosting the entire community for multiple days, erecting memorial megaliths (lung-thei), and carving house facades with ceremonial horn motifs.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 7: The Colonial Encounter and Political Awakenings
excerpts.tangkhul_text: The arrival of British administration in the late 19th century and the establishment of Rev. William Pettigrew's mission school at Ukhrul in 1896 initiated dramatic socioeconomic transformations. Roman script literacy, modern medical care, and Christianity gradually replaced the head-taking regime. Yet Tangkhul customary laws, land rights, and village identity endured, forming the foundation of modern Naga political consciousness and solidarity in northeast India.
excerpts.translation_en: British colonial administration and Rev. William Pettigrew's mission school in 1896 at Ukhrul catalyzed profound transformations. Roman literacy, healthcare, and Christianity gradually replaced the warfare regime. Yet customary laws, ancestral land tenure, and village identity endured, providing the bedrock of modern Naga political solidarity in northeast India.

front_matter.preface: Wung (Tangkhul) Naga Okthot Mayonza (Tangkhul Customary Law, Jurisprudence, and Social Ethics), compiled and authored by T. Luikham (Indigenous Scholar and Author, published at Imphal/Ukhrul, 1961). The definitive native codification of Tangkhul legal philosophy, matrimonial codes, clan inheritance, trials by ordeal, sanctuary rights, and compensatory restitution.

chapters.title: The Jurisprudential Philosophy of Wung Law
chapters.summary: Core principles of restorative justice: cosmic equilibrium (shak-kasa), communal restitution, and clan liability.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Wung (Tangkhul) customary law does not distinguish rigidly between civil tort and criminal injury; every offense is understood as a breach of cosmic and communal equilibrium (shak-kasa). The primary goal of judicial proceedings is not punitive incarceration, but the restitution of social harmony through compensatory settlement (shiman). Law is rooted in three principles: Respect for Ancestral Covenant (Khararchanwui Tuingashit), Preservation of Clan Integrity (Shangwui Kaphung), and Absolute Truthfulness before Varivara. The clan stands collective surety for its members.
chapters.english_translation: Wung customary law does not distinguish rigidly between tort and crime; every offense is a breach of cosmic equilibrium (shak-kasa). The primary goal is restorative harmony through compensatory settlement (shiman) rather than punitive incarceration. Law rests on three pillars: ancestral covenants, clan integrity, and truthfulness before God. The clan bears collective liability.

vocabulary.meaning: breach of taboo, disrupting communal balance
corporate clan honor and collective standing

chapters.grammar_notes: The abstract noun 'mayonza' derives from root 'mayon' (to watch over / govern responsibly) + '-za' (statute).

exercises.question: What is the primary objective of judicial proceedings in Wung customary law?
How does clan solidarity function regarding civil liabilities and fines?

chapters.title: Marriage Laws (Ngalong), Alliances, and Bride Wealth
chapters.summary: Strict clan exogamy, matrilateral cross-cousin alliances, bride wealth (shiman) protocols, and divorce penalties.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Marriage is an alliance between two distinct clans (shang). Strict exogamy is enforced under pain of grave moral censure. Marriage with a maternal aunt's daughter or mother's clan was preferred (cross-cousin marriage), cementing alliances. Bride wealth among the Tangkhul is not a commercial transaction, but a symbolic recompense to the bride's clan for the loss of her productive labor. Typical gifts include cattle (se), brass gongs (sen-kuir), and shawls. Divorce was uncommon and subject to rigorous financial penalties and property restitution.
chapters.english_translation: Marriage is an alliance between two distinct clans under strict exogamy. Cross-cousin marriage cemented bilateral ties. Bride wealth was a symbolic recompense for the loss of female labor, consisting of cattle, brass gongs, and handwoven textiles. Divorce was rare and penalized by stringent property forfeitures and subsistence indemnities.

vocabulary.meaning: valuable brass ceremonial gong used in bride wealth
formal betrothal negotiation between clan spokesmen
dowry possessions brought by the bride

chapters.grammar_notes: The nominal compound 'sen-kuir' fuses 'sen' (brass / bell-metal) with 'kuir' (circular rim / gong).

exercises.question: Why was cross-cousin marriage favored in traditional Tangkhul society?
What customary articles constituted bride wealth in Luikham's documentation?

chapters.title: Clan Inheritance (Kashak) and Land Tenures
chapters.summary: Inalienability of ancestral terrace fields, right of preemption by clan brethren, and primogeniture obligations.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Terrace land (Luingam) is held in perpetuity by lineages. Under no circumstance may ancestral land be sold to an outsider from another village. If an individual must alienate land due to debt, he must first offer the right of preemption to his nearest clan brethren (shangwui ngacham-mi). The eldest son (kaphung-mayar) inherits the ancestral home (shim-kharar) and principal terrace fields, assuming the obligation of maintaining aging parents and performing funeral rites. Younger sons receive secondary plots and assistance in constructing independent homesteads.
chapters.english_translation: Terrace land (Luingam) is held in perpetuity by lineages and can never be alienated to outside villagers. Preemption rights belong strictly to nearest clan brethren. The eldest son inherits the ancestral home and fields, assuming the solemn duty of caring for aged parents and funding funeral rites. Younger sons receive subordinate shares.

vocabulary.meaning: ancestral home, the elder family hearth
eldest son, principal heir and hearth keeper
funeral rites and ceremonial obligations for deceased parents

chapters.grammar_notes: The kinship term 'kaphung-mayar' signifies literally 'the son who bears the lineage weight' ('phung' = carry).

exercises.question: State the rule of preemption governing Tangkhul terrace fields.
What specific duties fall upon the eldest son under primogeniture?

chapters.title: Civil Wrongs, Thefts, and Restitution (Shiman)
chapters.summary: The threefold restitution rule for animal theft, grain theft penalties, and mediation of accidental injuries.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Theft of domestic animals was punished by threefold restitution (thum-ngashit): returning the stolen beast plus two additional animals of equal value as fine (kashiman) to the aggrieved family, plus a cleansing pig to the village council. Theft of harvested grain from field granaries was regarded as an aggravated offense requiring immediate public apology and heavy indemnity. Accidental physical injury was compensated according to working days lost, with the responsible party supplying rice and fowl. Homicide required temporary banishment to avert blood vengeance, followed by Pukreila peace negotiations.
chapters.english_translation: Theft of domestic animals was punished by threefold restitution (thum-ngashit): returning the animal plus two others as fine, with a cleansing pig for the council. Granary theft required public apology and heavy indemnity. Accidental injuries were compensated based on lost working days and medicinal supplies. Homicide necessitated temporary exile to avert vengeance.

vocabulary.meaning: public apology, ceremonial reconciliation before council

chapters.grammar_notes: Numeral compound 'thum-ngashit' combines 'thum' (three) with 'ngashit' (equal fold / multiplied measure).

exercises.question: Explain the formula of 'thum-ngashit' for livestock theft.
Why was granary theft considered an aggravated offense against the village?

chapters.title: Judicial Oaths and Trial by Ordeal (Theishak)
chapters.summary: Trial by ordeal when evidence fails: tiger tooth oaths, water immersion diving (tara-kachung), and divine judgment.
chapters.tangkhul_text: When oral testimony conflicted and evidence was inconclusive, the Hangva administered judicial oaths (theishak). An oath was not taken lightly; invoking false testimony before Varivara or clan ancestors was believed to result in premature death or the extinction of the swearer's lineage. The most solemn oath involved biting a tiger's tooth (shilwui ha) or touching a spear point. In property boundary disputes, contestants submitted to water immersion ordeals (tara-kachung), diving simultaneously into a river pool; the individual who surfaced first was adjudged dishonest. Hot water tests were also administered under the village priest's scrutiny.
chapters.english_translation: When testimony conflicted, the Hangva administered judicial oaths (theishak). False oaths before God or ancestors were believed to bring premature death or lineage extinction. Solemn oaths included biting a tiger's tooth or holding a spear point. Boundary disputes were decided by water immersion ordeals (tara-kachung); the contestant surfacing first lost the case.

vocabulary.meaning: judicial oath, solemn ordeal, invocation of divine judgment
tiger's tooth used in swearing supreme oaths
water immersion ordeal, competitive diving under river water
extinction of lineage as consequence of perjury

chapters.grammar_notes: The verbal noun 'tara-kachung' derives from 'tara' (water) and 'kachung' (entering / submerging deeply).

exercises.question: What metaphysical consequences were believed to follow false oaths in Tangkhul law?
Describe the procedural rules of the 'tara-kachung' water ordeal.

chapters.title: Traditional Taboos (Khamthei) and Sanctuary Rights
chapters.summary: Sacred rest days (genna / khamthei), the sanctuary of the chief's central pillar (shim-chui), and hearth purification.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Certain days were declared Khamthei (sacred rest days / genna) during which agricultural labor, weaving, and woodchopping were strictly forbidden. Breaching Khamthei was believed to blight crops and attracted village fines. The homestead of the Awunga served as an inviolable sanctuary. A fugitive fleeing vengeance who succeeded in touching the Awunga's central house-pillar (shim-chui) was granted temporary immunity while elders convened to arbitrate. Following unnatural deaths, purification ceremonies (shim-kashak) were conducted by the village Maiba before normal commensality could resume.
chapters.english_translation: Certain days were declared Khamthei (sacred genna days) where all labor was forbidden. Breaching taboos blighted crops and drew fines. The chief's home was an inviolable sanctuary; a fugitive touching the central pillar (shim-chui) gained immunity pending arbitration. Unnatural deaths required ritual house-cleansing (shim-kashak) by the priest before social commensality was restored.

vocabulary.meaning: taboo, sacred non-working day, genna restriction
central house-pillar, sacred pillar of sanctuary
ritual purification of hearth following defilement
unnatural death, demise by lightning, predator, or cliff fall

chapters.grammar_notes: Stative verb 'khamthei' (to be forbidden / set apart) nominalizes into the general term for taboo.

exercises.question: What physical act granted a fugitive temporary immunity from vengeance?
Describe the ceremonies conducted after an unnatural death ('khamatei thi').

chapters.title: Village Administration and Modern Legal Recognition
chapters.summary: Customary dues of the Awunga, codification under Manipur Hill Peoples Regulation (1947), and contemporary customary courts.
chapters.tangkhul_text: The Awunga was endowed with customary prerogatives: he received the right thigh of all game felled in village forests, was entitled to communal labor on his fields during the sowing season, and received a portion of adjudication fines. In exchange, the Awunga maintained the village covenant stones and represented the community in external treaties. Under the Manipur State Hill Peoples Regulation (1947), Tangkhul customary courts were granted formal statutory recognition to adjudicate civil and customary disputes, preserving speedy, restorative, and cost-free community justice.
chapters.english_translation: The Awunga received the right thigh of game felled in forests, communal labor on his fields, and judicial fine portions. In return, he maintained covenant stones and represented the village diplomatically. Under the Manipur State Hill Peoples Regulation (1947), customary courts received formal statutory recognition, ensuring restorative, cost-free justice.

vocabulary.meaning: customary tribute due to the chief (game thigh, field labor)
covenant stones erected at village boundaries
1947 statutory act recognizing tribal customary courts
just and equitable administration of customary law

chapters.grammar_notes: Noun phrase 'Tuingashit lung' joins 'tuingashit' (covenant) and 'lung' (stone megalith).

exercises.question: What customary tributes were historically rendered to the Tangkhul Awunga?
How did the 1947 Regulation protect indigenous tribal jurisprudence?

pages.header: Chapter 6: Traditional Taboos (Khamthei) and Sanctuary Rights (Page 16)
pages.title: Chapter 6: Traditional Taboos (Khamthei) and Sanctuary Rights
lines: CHAPTER 6: TRADITIONAL TABOOS (KHAMTHEI) AND SANCTUARY RIGHTS
Summary: Sacred rest days (genna / khamthei), the sanctuary of the chief's central pillar (shim-chui), and hearth purification.
Certain days were declared Khamthei (sacred rest days / genna) during
which agricultural labor, weaving, and woodchopping were strictly
forbidden. Breaching Khamthei was believed to blight crops and attracted
village fines. The homestead of the Awunga served as an inviolable
sanctuary. A fugitive fleeing vengeance who succeeded in touching the
Awunga's central house-pillar (shim-chui) was granted temporary immunity
while elders convened to arbitrate. Following unnatural deaths,
purification ceremonies (shim-kashak) were conducted by the village
Maiba before normal commensality could resume.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 1: The Jurisprudential Philosophy of Wung Law
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Wung (Tangkhul) customary law does not distinguish rigidly between civil tort and criminal injury; every offense is understood as a breach of cosmic and communal equilibrium (shak-kasa). The primary goal of judicial proceedings is not punitive incarceration, but the restitution of social harmony through compensatory settlement (shiman). Law is rooted in three principles: Respect for Ancestral Covenant (Khararchanwui Tuingashit), Preservation of Clan Integrity (Shangwui Kaphung), and Absolute Truthfulness before Varivara. The clan stands collective surety for its members.
excerpts.translation_en: Wung customary law does not distinguish rigidly between tort and crime; every offense is a breach of cosmic equilibrium (shak-kasa). The primary goal is restorative harmony through compensatory settlement (shiman) rather than punitive incarceration. Law rests on three pillars: ancestral covenants, clan integrity, and truthfulness before God. The clan bears collective liability.

front_matter.preface: Tangkhul Folk Ballads and Oral Narratives (Wungram Khararchan), collected, transcribed, and translated by Prof. Khashim Ruivah (Tribal Research Institute, Government of Manipur, Imphal, 1993). An authentic field collection of traditional folk poetry (Haola), including ancestral epics of Luikham and Raikham, seed-sowing chants of Luira, romantic courting duets (Mawonzai), hunting incantations, and funeral dirges (Kathi La) with parallel English translations.

chapters.title: Epic Ballads of Ancestral Heroes (Luikham and Raikham)
chapters.summary: Communal epic commemorating the ancestral founders clearing the ancient forests of Shirui Peak and eastern ranges.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Shirui kashongli kashung thot, Luikham mayarna thing-chui sathei; Shangwui khonkhur kachiva ngasoda, Wungram khararchan mathan salu! Khanggo shongli zattang thotna, Khayeikatha tara khorli; Meithei ramli ngaso-chithei, Raikham mayarna phara pamsai. The metre follows the traditional heptasyllabic cadence (seven syllables per line) typical of classical Tangkhul folk poetry, with internal rhyme and paired metaphorical couplets (tui-ngatei).
chapters.english_translation: On the high ridge of Shirui Peak, Hero Luikham felled the sacred tree; All the clans gathered with one voice, Singing the praise of the ancestral land! As they journeyed toward the eastern valleys, beside the clear sparkling streams, Brother Raikham established peaceful commerce with the peoples of the plains, cementing ancestral brotherhood. Classical heptasyllabic metre with paired metaphorical couplets.

vocabulary.meaning: Shirui Peak, highest sacred mountain in Ukhrul
sacred forest tree, central ridge timber
voice, resonant vocal harmony, clan assembly
paired metaphorical couplet, synonymous poetic parallelism

chapters.grammar_notes: Tangkhul classical poetry uses heptasyllabic (7-syllable) lines ending with prolonged vowel morae.

chapters.title: Agricultural Chants of Luira and Chumpha
chapters.summary: Chants for the February seed-sowing festival (Luira), monsoon terrace weeding, and post-harvest thanksgiving (Chumpha).
chapters.tangkhul_text: Luira phanit rarang thotna, Luingam ngaleili raruikatha chitheilu; Varivara kaphungli khangamor, Zingkum hili rui-kashang phanlu! Phaphuk ngashingda lui-kaphitli, Ngala-mayar ngasoda vangasai; Thangkhamir kachangli khangarao, Kong-khor tara mangda ngasolu! Chumpha phanit kasang thotna, Raizan shimli kashung kaping; Ava-ayi shiman mathailakla, Miwung kachivali tingkhami phanlu!
chapters.english_translation: When Luira festival draws near, present the seed of life to the terrace field; Praying to Almighty God on high, May this new year bring a bountiful harvest! With sturdy feet in muddy terrace waters, youth and maidens labor side by side; Though parched by midday sun, we drink of mountain streams together! When Chumpha feast arrives, granaries are filled to overflowing; let no household suffer want, and may peace dwell with all the people.

vocabulary.meaning: weeding of terrace paddy fields in monsoon

chapters.grammar_notes: Optative imperative suffix '-lu' on 'phanlu' functions as a collective prayer: may it bring blessing!

exercises.question: What three stages of the agricultural year are celebrated in these chants?
Translate the Chumpha festival couplet into English.

chapters.title: Romantic Courting Dialogues (Mawonzai)
chapters.summary: Nocturnal poetic duets at the girls' dormitory (Ngala Longshim) using floral and bird allegories.
chapters.tangkhul_text: The Suitor's Verse (Mayarwui La): 'Kazing kashungli won-kapha, Ngalawui maiwon theisai; Iwui malungli khayangna, Nali kongashi phunglikha.' The Maiden's Response (Ngalawui Ngahan): 'Shirui wonna kachang phungsai, Kha mayar nawui tuichi kashung; Shangwui khararbing ngashon-khalakha, Iwui malungli tingkhami phanlu.' Courtship was conducted through intricate metaphorical riddles, where direct speech was avoided in favor of floral allegories.
chapters.english_translation: Suitor: 'Upon the mountain heights blossoms a fair flower, I behold the maiden's radiant countenance; Looking into my heart, I bear deep love for you.' Maiden: 'The Shirui Lily blooms on high, yet young man, your words ring true; If the elders of the clans grant blessing, peace shall find a home within my heart.' Courtship duets avoided direct speech in favor of floral allegories.

vocabulary.meaning: romantic folk dialogue, courting poetry duet
the Shirui Lily (Lilium mackliniae), botanical emblem

chapters.grammar_notes: Metaphorical pairing of 'Shirui won' (rare endemic lily) symbolizes the prized virtue of the maiden.

exercises.question: Where were Mawonzai courting dialogues traditionally performed?
Analyze how botanical allegories replace direct romantic declarations in Tangkhul poetry.

chapters.title: Hunting Incantations and Forest Anthems (Khamasung La)
chapters.summary: Invocations to forest spirits (Khara-kameo), pursuit of wild quarry, and the serow triumph chant.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Ngashan phungli kapei khangaran, Khara-kameoli dori khami; Shi-wung kachangli khanasung, Awungali share khayao salu! Kaphung kachangli kashung sayat, Haophi kachonli mathan theikahai; Pangmashan mayarna theisatkatha, Longshimli la kashak phanlu! Upon felling wild game (stag, boar, serow), the hunting party sounded the victory horn (tala-khon) and entered the village gates singing triumphant chants. The right thigh was delivered to the Awunga.
chapters.english_translation: Ascending the ridges in preparation, presenting gifts to the forest spirits; Entering the dense mountain forest, Render the chief's rightful tribute! The serow roaming high cliffs has been struck down; Clothed in traditional cloth, its beauty displayed; The mighty youth have conquered; Let the dormitory raise the hunting song of triumph! The victory horn (tala-khon) accompanied entry into the village gates.

vocabulary.meaning: traditional Tangkhul woven cloth / warrior mantle

chapters.grammar_notes: The honorific compound 'shi-wung' combines 'shi' (wild beast) with 'wung' (majesty / sovereign of game).

exercises.question: What animal tribute was delivered to the Awunga after a successful hunt?
What traditional musical instrument announced the return of the hunting party?

chapters.title: Funeral Elegies and Laments (Kathi La)
chapters.summary: Guiding the departed soul along the trail to Kazeiram (the underworld realm of spirits) with ceremonial slit-drum rhythms.
chapters.tangkhul_text: I-va o, nawui zatkatha shongfali, Kazeiram kongli kaphan thotna; Khamatei ngathumli macharanlu, Khararbingna nali khaphung phungsai! Mourners beat the wooden slit-log drum (khamor-thing) in slow, syncopated rhythms accompanying the funeral chant. The dirge guides the soul past dangerous spiritual cliffs into the peaceful gathering place of the ancestors.
chapters.english_translation: O beloved father, along the path where you journey, When you reach the dark river of Kazeiram; Do not fear the shadow of the unknown, For the ancestors stand ready to welcome your soul! Mourners beat the wooden slit-log drum (khamor-thing) in solemn rhythms guiding the soul to the ancestral realm.

vocabulary.meaning: funeral elegy, death dirge, lamentation song
realm of departed souls, the ancestral underworld
departed spirit, soul of the deceased

chapters.grammar_notes: The vocative interjection 'I-va o' (O my father!) introduces profound filial grief in elegiac poetry.

exercises.question: What is Kazeiram in Tangkhul eschatological belief?
What musical instrument accompanies the recitation of Kathi La?

chapters.title: Martial Anthems and Victory Ballads (Rai La)
chapters.summary: War songs of defense, invocation of lineage bravery, and the solemn spear burial peacemaking finale.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Wungram kashangli kachisobing, Kachu-kaphi pangli phungda vangasai; Rari-kapangna raranglikha, Ithumwui ramli mazanglak mana! Following conflict, warriors assembled with their adversaries under the guidance of the Pukreila to sing the solemn reconciliation hymn, burying spearheads in the earth and swearing eternal non-aggression.
chapters.english_translation: Defenders of the noble homeland, marching forth with spear and shield in hand; Though enemies approach, they shall never enter our village territory! Following conflict, combatants gathered under the Pukreila's mediation to sing the reconciliation hymn, burying spearheads in the earth in eternal peace covenants.

vocabulary.meaning: martial anthem, war song, defense hymn
shall never enter, absolutely barred entry

chapters.grammar_notes: Emphatic prohibitive suffix combination '-lak mana' denotes resolute defensive determination.

exercises.question: What armaments are described in the warrior's verse?
How did martial songs transition into peacemaking ceremonies?

chapters.title: Proverbs and Moral Allegories in Song (Paotam La)
chapters.summary: Tribal philosophy in lyrical proverbs: agricultural diligence, clan obedience, and ethical rectitude.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Folk singers embedded tribal philosophy into short lyrical proverbs (Paotam La) taught to children around winter fires: 'Khamatei sachitheikha maram kashung mathailak mana' (A crooked beginning cannot yield an upright crop). 'Shangwui tuili ngashon-katha kazing kashungli pamsai' (He who heeds clan counsel walks under clear skies). 'Luingamli mik kachangna raizanli raruikatha theilikha' (Eyes that watch the terrace fields will see full granaries). The volume concludes with critical musical apparatus: pentatonic scales, antiphonal Mawonzai structures, and funeral metres.
chapters.english_translation: Tribal philosophy was embedded in memorable lyrical proverbs taught around evening fires: A crooked start yields no upright crop; He who heeds clan counsel walks under open skies; Eyes watchful over terrace fields shall behold overflowing granaries. Critical apparatus includes pentatonic scales, antiphonal structures, and elegiac drum metres.

vocabulary.meaning: ancient folk chant on pentatonic scale

chapters.grammar_notes: Proverbial conditional '-khalakha' pairs ethical cause with inevitable agricultural or social consequence.

exercises.question: Translate the proverb 'Shangwui tuili ngashon-katha kazing kashungli pamsai' and interpret its cultural meaning.
Summarize the metric features of classical Tangkhul folk poetry documented by Ruivah.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 1: Epic Ballads of Ancestral Heroes (Luikham and Raikham)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Shirui kashongli kashung thot, Luikham mayarna thing-chui sathei; Shangwui khonkhur kachiva ngasoda, Wungram khararchan mathan salu! Khanggo shongli zattang thotna, Khayeikatha tara khorli; Meithei ramli ngaso-chithei, Raikham mayarna phara pamsai. The metre follows the traditional heptasyllabic cadence (seven syllables per line) typical of classical Tangkhul folk poetry, with internal rhyme and paired metaphorical couplets (tui-ngatei).
excerpts.translation_en: On the high ridge of Shirui Peak, Hero Luikham felled the sacred tree; All the clans gathered with one voice, Singing the praise of the ancestral land! As they journeyed toward the eastern valleys, beside the clear sparkling streams, Brother Raikham established peaceful commerce with the peoples of the plains, cementing ancestral brotherhood. Classical heptasyllabic metre with paired metaphorical couplets.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 2: Agricultural Chants of Luira and Chumpha
excerpts.tangkhul_text: Luira phanit rarang thotna, Luingam ngaleili raruikatha chitheilu; Varivara kaphungli khangamor, Zingkum hili rui-kashang phanlu! Phaphuk ngashingda lui-kaphitli, Ngala-mayar ngasoda vangasai; Thangkhamir kachangli khangarao, Kong-khor tara mangda ngasolu! Chumpha phanit kasang thotna, Raizan shimli kashung kaping; Ava-ayi shiman mathailakla, Miwung kachivali tingkhami phanlu!
excerpts.translation_en: When Luira festival draws near, present the seed of life to the terrace field; Praying to Almighty God on high, May this new year bring a bountiful harvest! With sturdy feet in muddy terrace waters, youth and maidens labor side by side; Though parched by midday sun, we drink of mountain streams together! When Chumpha feast arrives, granaries are filled to overflowing; let no household suffer want, and may peace dwell with all the people.

excerpts.chapter: Chapter 3: Romantic Courting Dialogues (Mawonzai)
excerpts.tangkhul_text: The Suitor's Verse (Mayarwui La): 'Kazing kashungli won-kapha, Ngalawui maiwon theisai; Iwui malungli khayangna, Nali kongashi phunglikha.' The Maiden's Response (Ngalawui Ngahan): 'Shirui wonna kachang phungsai, Kha mayar nawui tuichi kashung; Shangwui khararbing ngashon-khalakha, Iwui malungli tingkhami phanlu.' Courtship was conducted through intricate metaphorical riddles, where direct speech was avoided in favor of floral allegories.
excerpts.translation_en: Suitor: 'Upon the mountain heights blossoms a fair flower, I behold the maiden's radiant countenance; Looking into my heart, I bear deep love for you.' Maiden: 'The Shirui Lily blooms on high, yet young man, your words ring true; If the elders of the clans grant blessing, peace shall find a home within my heart.' Courtship duets avoided direct speech in favor of floral allegories.

chapters.title: Matthew Kahona Kasa: The Nativity & The Beatitudes
chapters.summary: The genealogy of Christ and the historic Sermon on the Mount Beatitudes rendered into Tangkhul.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Matthew 5:3-10: Mangazingli ngachamkakhui bingna mathasek-u, kasakei kazingram athumwuisai. Khangaringli ngachirbingna mathasek-u, kasakei athumli khangasak milu sara. Khamanoubingna mathasek-u, kasakei athum mikumo ngaleili ngashansara. Mashung-kasa vang kachamkashi bingna mathasek-u, athumna thingkhalara. Khangacham thotli ngashanbingna mathasek-u, athumli ngashan milu sara.
chapters.english_translation: Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth. Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled. Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
grammar_notes: Suffix -bing marks nominal plurality (ngachirbing = those who mourn).
Optative imperative/blessing suffix -sek-u expresses solemn blessing ('mathasek-u' = blessed be).
exercises: Translate Matthew 5:3 into contemporary spoken Tangkhul.
Identify the grammatical particles functioning as emphatic markers in verse 7.

chapters.title: John Kahona Kasa: The Incarnation & The Light of Men
chapters.summary: Prologue of John in classic Tangkhul syntax, exploring the theological rendering of 'Word' (Tui).
chapters.tangkhul_text: Kaphung-kachungwui thotli Tui li-li-sai, kala Tuichi Varivarali lei, kala Tuichi Varivarasai. Chiya kaphung-kachungli Varivarawui kachungli leisai. Ali vangteina ot kathata pamei sakahaisai; kala sachitheikahai thotwui tharili A matheida khikha masasa mana. Ali ringkapha lei, kala ringkapha china mikumowui mangashan phāsa-e. Kala mangashan chi ngashingli ngashane, kala ngashingna chi mathakakhui-mana.
chapters.english_translation: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.

vocabulary.meaning: the very beginning, dawn of creation

grammar_notes: Reduplication 'li-li-sai' indicates continuous remote past existence.
Negative verbal frame 'ma-...-mana' in 'mathakakhui-mana' (did not comprehend/overcome).
exercises: Examine the cultural adoption of 'Tui' (word, message, discourse) for Logos in early Tangkhul literature.
Identify the case endings on 'Varivara' (God).

chapters.title: The Acts of the Apostles: Pentecost & The First Fellowship
chapters.summary: The descent of the Holy Spirit and early communal living described in Ukhrul dialect.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Acts 2:1-4: Pentecostwui phanit atamli athumpup ngalem akhali ngaburkapam leisai. Chitharan khamathān kazingwui eina hu-hu kaho khongyui kakhangahui akhata rarer, kala athum pamkapam shim tharili chuiserie. Kala athumli meikazat theirei katha tuitak thada kashikaza theiser, kala athum akhakha wui tuingalungli pamserie. Kala athumpup Kazing Mangazing Katharana phāserlaga, kapei tui katek-tek eina tui khangayei honserie.
chapters.english_translation: When the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues.

chapters.title: Linguistic & Orthographic Lexicon of the 1927 Translation
chapters.summary: Systematic glossary of 50 key loanwords, calques, and dialectal roots documented in the 1927 text.
chapters.tangkhul_text:
Tangkhul Kathara Lairik Tuitam:
1. Varivara -- Almighty Supreme God (traditional Christianized deity term)
2. Kazingram -- Heaven / celestial dominion
3. Mangazing Kathara -- Holy Spirit
4. Naomayār -- Beloved Son
5. Khangayei -- Divine love / agape
6. Mashung-kasa -- Righteousness / moral integrity
7. Kazingkaphung -- Persecution / adversity
8. Chotkhangashit -- Faith / steadfast belief
9. Ngachikan -- Hope / sacred expectation
10. Shillong Kathara -- Holy City / heavenly sanctuary
chapters.english_translation: A comprehensive gloss of theological, moral, and structural Tangkhul terms compiled from the 1927 New Testament, serving as a landmark milestone in the linguistic history of Manipur.
grammar_notes: Historical orthography: usage of 'wui' for genitive instead of modern shortened forms.
Phonetic preservation of final stops and bilabial glides.
exercises: Compare 10 words from this lexicon with their modern counterparts in the TLS 2021 curriculum.
Trace how the word 'Varivara' shifted in semantic domain during the 20th century.

pages.title: John Kahona Kasa: The Incarnation & The Light of Men
lines: CHAPTER 2: JOHN KAHONA KASA: THE INCARNATION & THE LIGHT OF MEN
Summary: Prologue of John in classic Tangkhul syntax, exploring the theological rendering...
Kaphung-kachungwui thotli Tui li-li-sai, kala Tuichi Varivarali lei,
kala Tuichi Varivarasai. Chiya kaphung-kachungli Varivarawui kachungli
leisai. Ali vangteina ot kathata pamei sakahaisai; kala sachitheikahai
thotwui tharili A matheida khikha masasa mana. Ali ringkapha lei, kala
ringkapha china mikumowui mangashan phāsa-e. Kala mangashan chi
ngashingli ngashane, kala ngashingna chi mathakakhui-mana.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word
was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by
him; and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was
life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in
darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.

rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were

and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy
Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues.

chapters.title: The Genealogy and Nativity of Christ (Matthew 1-2)
chapters.summary: The generational lineage and the arrival of the Wise Men in Bethlehem rendered in Tangkhul.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Matthew 1:18-21: Jesu Christawui kaphari hithada leisai: Awui ava Maryli Joseph eina phankahai ngachaoda maleiranglakha, ana Kazing Mangazing Katharawui eina phasa kapang theitserie. Chitharan awui va Josephna mikumo mashungna kahana, ali kakhana phasa maleiranglakha khangareili zanglaga kashang-phā eina thang-khavai ning khami leisai. Kala ana naomayār akha sashapra, kala nawui eina ali JESU hoda kahang sara, kasakei Ana awui mikumoli athumwui yorshi eina huikhui sara.
chapters.english_translation: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost. Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily. And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
grammar_notes: Postposition 'ngachaoda' indicates temporal precedence ('prior to', 'before').
Causative verbal suffix '-shuk' or future volitional '-sara' (huikhui sara = shall redeem/save).
exercises: Identify the Tangkhul verb corresponding to 'espoused / betrothed'.
Explain the morphological derivation of 'huikhui' (to rescue/save).

chapters.title: The Lord's Prayer & The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6)
chapters.summary: The classic Lord's Prayer (Ithui Kaphungli Kasa Ava) and ethical teachings on prayer and fasting.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Matthew 6:9-13: Chiwui vang nathumna hithada haikaphā salu: 'Ithui kazingramli kaphung Ava, Nawui ming katharaseru. Nawui ngashan kasakazing raseru. Nawui ningkazang kazingramli thada ngaleili ngasokalu. Ithuli tharan kashakhavai kachak zingsho zingsho ithuli milu. Kala ithumna ithuli kashikashili ngashankahaimi thada, ithuwui yorshili ngashankahaimilu. Kala ithuli kakhayangli makaso-alu, kashikashili huikhuilu; kasakei ngashankasakazing, kala pangashan, kala phashan chinawui kuppup thotli nawuisai. Amen.'
chapters.english_translation: After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.
grammar_notes: Direct imperative suffix '-lu' on verbal stems: salu (do/pray!), milu (give!), huikhuilu (deliver!).
Prohibitive negative imperative: 'ma-...-alu' in 'makaso-alu' (do not lead!).
exercises: Recite the Lord's Prayer in Tangkhul from memory.
Compare the term 'pangashan' (power) with 'phashan' (glory).

chapters.title: Parables of the Kingdom of Heaven (Matthew 13)
chapters.summary: The Parable of the Sower and the Pearl of Great Price in rural agricultural Tangkhul imagery.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Matthew 13:3-8: 'Theilu, kachit kasana chitchikhavai vaye. Kala ana chitkhalangli, charakha shongzali tuksangie, kala vanaona rarlaga shaksangserie. Charakha ngalung thotli tuksangie, chithuili ngalei kachung malei; kala ngalei maleiranglakha khangateili phayokaserie. Kha zinga rar-daran chi meiratsangie, kala ngari maleimana chiwui vang kangsangserie. Charakha suh thotli tuksangie, kala suhna shoklaga pomsangserie. Kha charakha ngalei kaphāli tuksangie, kala theirarlaga akha eina thakharā, akha eina tharuk-magā, akha eina magā thotna.'
chapters.english_translation: Behold, a sower went forth to sow; And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up: Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away. And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them: But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.
grammar_notes: Agricultural classifier constructions: 'charakha' (some, a portion).
Multiplication idioms: 'akha eina thakharā' (one producing a hundredfold).
exercises: How does the Tangkhul translation convey the four types of soil?
What verb root expresses 'to wither away'?

chapters.title: The Golden Rule & The Narrow Gate (Matthew 7)
chapters.summary: Practical ethical guidance: judging others, seeking wisdom, and the narrow gate to life.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Matthew 7:7-14: 'Hanglu, chitharan nathumli misara; khayorlu, chitharan nathumna phāsara; shimkakhong kakorlu, chitharan nathumli hungkahang misara. Kachikathāna hangkakhui thapup khuiye; kala khayorkakhui thapup phāye; kala kakorkakhuili hungkahang miye. Khong kakatli zanglu; kasakei khong khangashir kala shongfa kakhangashir china kashili vashukana, kala zangkakhui bing kachungsai. Kha khong kakat kala shongfa kaphā china ringkaphali vashukana, kala chichi phākakhui bing kachamlakna.'
chapters.english_translation: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you: For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.

vocabulary.meaning: to knock, rap on the gate

grammar_notes: Correlative paired clauses: 'hanglu... misara' (ask... it shall be given).
Antonyms in Tangkhul ethics: 'kasham/kashi' (destruction) vs 'ringkapha' (life).
exercises: Translate Matthew 7:12 (The Golden Rule) into written Tangkhul.
Identify the imperative markers used in the exhortation.

chapters.title: The Transfiguration & Healing (Matthew 17)
chapters.summary: Christ's transfiguration on the high mountain and the healing of the afflicted youth.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Matthew 17:1-5: Zing kum tharuk ngaphalaga, Jesuna Peter, James, kala awui khanao Johnli kaphung kashang akhali athum kacham eina thukpingsangie. Kala athum mik-ngalemli Awui aphasa khangatei thotna: Awui mai zingkhamathān katha thada ngashangie, kala Awui kachon mangashan katha thada kachak-ngayei thotna. Kala theilu, athumli Moses kala Elijah tui-hanglakha theiserie.
chapters.english_translation: And after six days Jesus taketh Peter, James, and John his brother, and bringeth them up into an high mountain apart, And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light. And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him.
grammar_notes: Temporal sequential conjunction: 'zing kum tharuk ngaphalaga' (after six days had passed).
Color and radiance descriptive compound: 'kachak-ngayei' (radiantly white).
exercises: Discuss the cultural significance of 'kaphung' in Tangkhul geography and cosmology.
Identify the names of the three disciples in Tangkhul orthography.

chapters.title: The Great Commission & Epilogue (Matthew 28)
chapters.summary: The resurrection, triumph over death, and the universal apostolic commission.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Matthew 28:18-20: Kala Jesuna athum ngalemli rarlaga hangmi: 'Kazingram kala ngaleili pangashan kuppup ili miserie. Chiwui vang nathumna valaga mikumo ngashan pupup-li tuitam kasalu, Avawui, Naomayārwui, kala Kazing Mangazing Katharawui ming eina athumli baptism milu. Kala I nathumli sakasashikahai ot pupupli shurkhavai tuitam kasalu: kala theilu, I thotwui kashikhavai thada zingsho pupup nathum eina li-leisara. Amen.'
chapters.english_translation: And Jesus came and spake unto them, saying, All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth. Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.

vocabulary.meaning: end of the age, consummation of time

grammar_notes: Universal quantifier 'pupup' attached to nominals (ngashan pupup = all nations; ot pupup = all commands).
Continuous presence promise marked by future auxiliary: 'li-leisara' (shall continuously abide).
exercises: Examine how Pettigrew rendered the Trinitarian formula into Tangkhul.
Translate the Great Commission into modern Standard Tangkhul.

pages.english_translation: Behold, a sower went forth to sow; And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up: Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away. And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprung up, and choked them: But other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold.

title: Pa o Kamata Isha mai Jesu Christawui Khararchan: Mark Kahona Kasa
alternate_titles: The Gospel of St. Mark in Tangkhul Naga (1909)
publisher: British and Foreign Bible Society, Calcutta / Baptist Mission Press
subject: Biblical Literature & Vernacular Translation
notes: 1909 publication of St. Mark in Tangkhul Naga by Rev. William Pettigrew. Presents dynamic narrative prose, action-oriented discourse particles, and early linguistic orthography. Public Domain.

front_matter.title_page: Pa o Kamata Isha mai Jesu Christawui Khararchan: Mark Kahona Kasa (1909)
front_matter.preface: The Gospel of Mark is characterized by rapidity of action and direct vivid narration. Translated by William Pettigrew and published by BFBS in 1909. In Tangkhul, frequent narrative connectives like 'chitharan' (thereupon) and 'khamathān' (immediately) showcase vernacular verbal sequencing.
