chapters.title: The Ministry of John the Baptist & Baptism of Jesus (Mark 1)
chapters.summary: The voice crying in the wilderness and the opening of the gospel narrative in Tangkhul.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Mark 1:1-4: Jesu Christa, Varivarawui Naomayārwui khararchan kaphung: Isaiah kaho tui-theikhanana kasa thada leiri: 'Theilu, Nawui mik-ngalemli Iwui pao-phungnaoli kasho vaye, ana nawui shongfa ngalunghang sara. Ramkashilashili khongyui akhana hohe: 'Prohowui shongfa kapanglu, Awui lambili mashunglu.' Johnna ramkashilashili baptism kasami thotna, kala yorshi ngashankahavai ningkaphuritwui baptism pao phongie.
chapters.english_translation: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God; As it is written in the prophets, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee. The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. John did baptize in the wilderness, and preach the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.
grammar_notes: Quotative marker 'hohe' denoting direct proclamation.
Compound verb 'ngalunghang' (to prepare/clear completely).
exercises: Identify the prophetic title given to John the Baptist.
How is 'wilderness' lexicalized in Tangkhul?

chapters.title: The Stilling of the Storm (Mark 4)
chapters.summary: Miracle on the Sea of Galilee demonstrating authority over wind and waves in Tangkhul description.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Mark 4:35-41: Chi zingsho ngazing-tharan, Ana athumli hang: 'Ngashakazil kakahara kachili ithum ngakorva-u.' Kala mikumo kachungli kashikahailaga, A kuphungli leisai thada thukpingserie. Chitharan hu-hu kaho huimayon kasham akhata rarer, kala tui-ngachaona kuphung tharili ngashingye, chithada kuphung chi tui eina kashung thotna. Kala A kuphung wui kashikli mikazak akhali luipatlaga ngaphamsai: kala athumna ali pholaga hang: 'Tuitamkasana, ithum mathira chi Nawui ningli malei-macho?' Kala A shoklaga huili kaphangserie, kala ngashakazilli hang: 'Maza-lu, ngacham-lu!' Chitharan huichi ngachaoran thotna, kala chitharan ngakazil khamatha akhata shokserie.
chapters.english_translation: And the same day, when the even was come, he saith unto them, Let us pass over unto the other side. And when they had sent away the multitude, they took him even as he was in the ship. And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full. And he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow: and they awake him, and say unto him, Master, carest thou not that we perish? And he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
grammar_notes: Two-part imperative command: 'Maza-lu, ngacham-lu!' (Be silent, be peaceful!).
Ingressive aspectual particle: 'thotna' denoting rapid onset of state.
exercises: Contrast the terms for boat/canoe ('kuphung') and sea/lake ('ngashakazil').
Identify the verb for rebuking the elements ('kaphang').

chapters.title: The Feeding of the Five Thousand (Mark 6)
chapters.summary: Multiplication of the five loaves and two fishes in Tangkhul hospitality idiom.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Mark 6:38-44: Ana athumli hang: 'Nathumli raruikatha kaphara lei? Vayanglu.' Kala theilaga athumna hang: 'Phangā lei, kala ngachayei khani lei.' Ana athumpup-li haikaphā salaga kacham eina ngashalungli pamkazip milu hoda hangserie. Kala athum thakharā eina, phangā-magā eina ngaburlaga pamserie. Kala Ana raruikatha phangā chi kala ngachayei khani chi khuilaga, kazingli yanglaga Varivarali mathat-eina kashaklaga raruikatha chi khakserie; kala mikumo tharili shunsangserie. Kala athumpup shaksarlaga phasa kashung thotna.
chapters.english_translation: He saith unto them, How many loaves have ye? go and see. And when they knew, they say, Five, and two fishes. And he commanded them to make all sit down by companies upon the green grass. And they sat down in ranks, by hundreds, and by fifties. And when he had taken the five loaves and the two fishes, he looked up to heaven, and blessed, and brake the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before them. And they did all eat, and were filled.
grammar_notes: Distributive numerical expressions: 'thakharā eina, phangā-magā eina' (by hundreds, by fifties).
Completive satiety marker: 'phasa kashung thotna' (their bodies became completely satisfied).
exercises: How does Tangkhul express communal grouping during feasts?
What verb root describes blessing and breaking bread?

chapters.title: The Greatest Commandment & The Widow's Mite (Mark 12)
chapters.summary: Love for God and neighbor, alongside the sacrificial offering of the poor widow.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Mark 12:29-31, 42-44: Jesuna ngahanmi: 'Hingchithei kaphāmeina hi: O Israel, kapeilu; Proho ithui Varivara, Proho akhachana! Kala nawui lungkashung eina, nawui mangazing eina, nawui ning-kacham eina Proho nawui Varivarali ngayeilu: hi hingchithei khare. Kala khakhane chi hithada: 'Nawui aphasa thada nawui ngalemwui mikumoli ngayeilu.' ...Kala ngalashang kacham akha rarlaga paisa khani haksangie. Jesuna hang: 'Ngalashang hi ana kachikathāna haksangmeiserie; kasakei a kacham thotli awui ringkaphavai leikashap kuppup haksangserie.'
chapters.english_translation: And Jesus answered him, The first of all the commandments is, Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord: And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment. And the second is like, namely this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. ...And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites. And Jesus said, This poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury: For all they did cast in of their abundance; but she of her want did cast in all that she had, even all her living.
grammar_notes: Instrumental postposition 'eina' emphasizing holistic totality ('with all thy heart').
Comparative superiority: 'haksangmeiserie' (cast in far more than all).
exercises: Translate the summary of the Law into colloquial Tangkhul.
Explain the ethical significance of the widow's sacrificial giving.

chapters.title: The Resurrection & Final Commission (Mark 16)
chapters.summary: The empty tomb at sunrise and the mandate to proclaim good tidings everywhere.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Mark 16:1-6: Sabbath ngaphalaga, Mary Magdalene, Jameswui ava Mary, kala Salomena rarlaga Awui phasa kakhalaphavai meithei-chot khuisangserie. Kala hoptawui zingsho khareli, zingkhamathān shoklakha lungkhorli rarlakna. Kala theilu, lungphung kashang chi lunkhor khong eina khangayot theiserie. Kala lungkhor tharili zanglaga kashang-phā chon kachak kazang mayarnaowon akha pamsai theilaga athum ngachek-kashung thotna. Kha ana athumli hang: 'Mangachek-alu: Nazarethwui Jesu, thingkhamirangli kahom chi nathum khayore; A ngatekrarlaga thotsangie; A hili maleira: theilu, A pili kahai pam hi!'
chapters.english_translation: And when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they might come and anoint him. And very early in the morning the first day of the week, they came unto the sepulchre at the rising of the sun. And they saw that the stone was rolled away: for it was very great. And entering into the sepulchre, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a long white garment; and they were affrighted. And he saith unto them, Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.

vocabulary.meaning: having risen triumphantly, awakened from death

grammar_notes: Tangkhul neologism for Cross: 'thing' (wood) + 'khamirang' (crossed/scaffold) = thingkhamirang.
Prohibitive imperative: 'Mangachek-alu' (Do not be frightened).
exercises: Analyze the morphology of 'thingkhamirang'.
Trace the narrative arc from grief to proclamation in Mark 16.

chapters.title: Lexical Concordance of the Gospel of Mark
chapters.summary: Specialized vocabulary of action verbs, directional postpositions, and miracle terms in Mark.
chapters.tangkhul_text:
Tuiwon Kasakakhui:
1. Huimayon -- Tempestuous wind storm
2. Kuphung -- Sea boat / fishing canoe
3. Maza-lu -- Peace / silence (imperative)
4. Lungkhor -- Stone tomb / burial cavern
5. Thingkhamirang -- The Cross
6. Ngatekrarlaga -- Risen from the dead
7. Ningkaphurit -- Repentance of heart
8. Ramkashilashi -- Wilderness tract
chapters.english_translation: Action vocabulary and geographical terminology compiled from the 1909 translation of Mark.
grammar_notes: Narrative pacing markers: 'chitharan' vs 'khamathān'.
exercises: Write five sentences using the vocabulary of Mark 4.

khangayot theiserie. Kala lungkhor tharili zanglaga kashang-phā chon

And when the sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of
James, and Salome, had bought sweet spices, that they might come and
anoint him. And very early in the morning the first day of the week,
they came unto the sepulchre at the rising of the sun. And they saw that
the stone was rolled away: for it was very great. And entering into the
sepulchre, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a
long white garment; and they were affrighted. And he saith unto them, Be
not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is
risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.

title: Avara Kasa wui Khararchan: The Book of Genesis in Tangkhul Naga
alternate_titles: The Book of Genesis in Tangkhul Naga
publisher: Bible Society of India, Bangalore / Guwahati
subject: Biblical Literature & Vernacular Translation
notes: Standard Tangkhul translation of the Book of Genesis. Contains the foundational narratives of Creation, Eden, the Great Flood, Babel, and the Patriarchs in rich poetic Tangkhul.

front_matter.title_page: Avara Kasa wui Khararchan: The Book of Genesis in Tangkhul Naga (1965)
front_matter.preface: The Book of Genesis (Avara Kasa wui Khararchan) establishes the foundational cosmogony of the Tangkhul Bible. Translated and refined across successive generations by native scholars and the Bible Society of India, it bridges ancient Semitic narratives with the rich ecological and agrarian vocabulary of the Naga hills.

chapters.title: The Creation of the World (Genesis 1)
chapters.summary: The six days of creation and the Sabbath rest in grand ceremonial Tangkhul diction.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Genesis 1:1-5, 26-27: Kaphung-kachungwui thotli Varivarana kazing kala ngalei sakahaisai. Kala ngalei chi kasham eina khangari-leilakha leisai, kala ngaching china kapei ngashakazilli chumpamsai; kala Varivarawui Mangazingna tui-ngapomli ngazuklaga pamye. Chitharan Varivarana hang: 'Mangashan shokru!' Kala mangashan shokserie. Kala Varivarana mangashan kaphā chi theitserie, kala mangashan kala ngachingli kashit-eina pamsakserie. ...Kala Varivarana hang: 'Ithuwui mai thada, ithuwui katha eina mikumoli saru; athumna ngashakazilwui ngachayei, kazingramwui vanao, kala ngaleiwui saphang kuppupli ngashankasarap sara.' Hithada Varivarana Awui mai thada mikumoli sakahaisai; mayarnaowon kala ngalanaowon eina sakahaisai.
chapters.english_translation: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. ...And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth. So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

vocabulary.meaning: beasts of the earth, animal kingdom

grammar_notes: Divine fiat imperative formula: 'shokru!' (Let there be!).

chapters.title: Noah's Ark & The Rainbow Covenant (Genesis 6-9)
chapters.summary: The construction of the giant wooden vessel, the deluge, and the rainbow token of peace.

chapters.title: The Call of Abraham & The Covenant of Faith (Genesis 12 & 15)
chapters.summary: Abraham's departure from Ur and the promise of descendants numerous as the stars of heaven.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Genesis 12:1-3, 15:5: Prohona Abramli hang: 'Nawui ram, nawui shimanwui ngalung, kala nawui avashim eina shoklaga, I chitheikhavai ramli valoo! Kala I nawui eina ngashan kashang akha sarap sara, kala I nawui phāsan milu sara... kala nawui ming eina ngaleiwui ngashan pupupna mathāsek-u sara.' ...Ana Abramli kaphung eina yangsaklaga hang: 'Kazingli yanglu, sirabingli kharep-shukralang khareplu!' Kala Ana hang: 'Nawui ngashan chi hithada sara.' Kala Abramna Proholi chotkhangashit khuiye; kala chiya awui mashung-kasa hoda hisangmi.
chapters.english_translation: Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing: And in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. ...And he brought him forth abroad, and said, Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them: and he said unto him, So shall thy seed be. And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
grammar_notes: Direct imperative departure form: 'valoo!' (Go forth!).
Patrilineal kinship terminology: 'avashim' reflects native clan organization.

chapters.title: Joseph and His Brothers in Egypt (Genesis 37 & 45)
chapters.summary: The coat of many colors, the descent into Egypt, and the reconciliation of Joseph with his clan.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Genesis 37:3, 45:3-5: Israelna Josephli azao-azana tharili pamei ngayeiye; kala ana awui vang kachon kakhangatei kaphā akha sakahaisai. ...Josephna awui uningnaobingli hang: 'I Joseph-sai! I-ava ring-leirang-macho?' Kha uningnaobingna awui ngalemli ngachek-kashung thotlaga ngahan-mashuk-mana. Kala Josephna hang: 'I ngalemli rarlaklu... nathumna ili hili pashitsang-kaji vang ningkasham makasaloo: kasakei mikumowui ringkaphavai huikhuikhavai Varivarana ili nathumwui mik-ngalemli kashokahaisaye!'
chapters.english_translation: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours. ...And Joseph said unto his brethren, I am Joseph; doth my father yet live? And his brethren could not answer him; for they were troubled at his presence. And Joseph said unto his brethren, Come near to me, I pray you... Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.
grammar_notes: Prohibitive emotional phrase: 'ningkasham makasaloo' (Do not make grief of heart).
Sibling collective plural: 'uningnaobing' (older and younger brothers).
exercises: Discuss the emotional vocabulary in Joseph's reconciliation speech.
How does the concept of divine providence surface in Genesis 45:5?

In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And the earth was

the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.

I-ava ring-leirang-macho?' Kha uningnaobingna awui ngalemli ngachek-kashung thotlaga ngahan-mashuk-mana. Kala Josephna hang: 'I ngalemli rarlaklu... nathumna ili hili pashitsang-kaji vang ningkasham makasaloo: kasakei mikumowui ringkaphavai huikhuikhavai Varivarana ili nathumwui mik-ngalemli kashokahaisaye!'
pages.english_translation: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours. ...And Joseph said unto his brethren, I am Joseph; doth my father yet live? And his brethren could not answer him; for they were troubled at his presence. And Joseph said unto his brethren, Come near to me, I pray you... Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life.

chapters.title: Psalm 1: The Two Ways -- Tree by the Water Brooks
chapters.summary: Contrast between the righteous person flourishing like a river tree and the chaff blown by wind.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Psalm 1:1-4: Kaphā-kashana mikumo kachikhana kashikashibingwui ningkazangli mashurla, yorshibingwui shongfali mangapamla, kala khanganoibingwui pamkaphunli mangapam-mana; Kha ana Prohowui ngashan-kasakazingli mathat-eina leikashiye, kala Awui tui zingsho ngazing kachikhali thimkazape. Ana kongkha kaphā wui tui-ngapomli thingphun phunkahai thada sakhura, ana awui thotli thei kaphā phāser-ra, awui naorap mangapaorira; kala ana sakahai ot pupupli mashungsere. Kashikashibing chi hithada maleimana: kha huina shuk-kakhui pakhara thada kasaye.
chapters.english_translation: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful. But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper. The ungodly are not so: but are like the chaff which the wind driveth away.

vocabulary.meaning: threshing chaff, husks blown by breeze

grammar_notes: Three-fold negative parallel clauses: 'mashurla... mangapamla... mangapam-mana'.
Simile with botanical imagery: 'thingphun phunkahai thada' (like a tree planted).
exercises: Identify the botanical terms for leaf ('naorap') and fruit ('thei').
Contrast the righteous and ungodly using the imagery of Psalm 1.

chapters.title: Psalm 23: The Shepherd Psalm (Proho i-wui Ngashankashapana)
chapters.summary: The beloved pastoral psalm of comfort, protection, and overflowing blessing in lyrical Tangkhul.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Psalm 23:1-6: Proho i-wui Ngashankashapana; ili khikha macham-mana. Ana ili ngashalung kaphāli pamkazipsake, kala kongkhamathān tui-ngapomli ili zaipinge. Ana iwui mangazingli mathangathuksake: Awui mingwui vang mashung-kasa shongfali ili zaisange. I kathi ngachingwui longkhorli zakhalangli, I kashikashili mangachek-mana; kasakei Na i eina li-leie; Nawui thingchot kala deikhotna ili ngasot-e. Nawui mik-ngalemli i-kashibingwui ngalemli maihon akha sakahaye; Nawui eina iwui kakhutli meirong theiye; iwui kom kashunglaga tuksange. Mashungna iwui ringkapha tharili kaphā kala ngashan china ili shursara: kala i Prohowui shimli thot khamara kuppup pamkapamsara.
chapters.english_translation: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreeth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.

vocabulary.meaning: deep ravine, mountain gorge, shadow valley

grammar_notes: Agentive personal title with suffix '-na': 'Ngashankashapana' (The One who shepherds).
Highland geographical term for valley: 'longkhor' (deep mountain ravine).
exercises: Recite Psalm 23 in Tangkhul verse.
How is 'my cup runneth over' expressed in Tangkhul?

chapters.title: Psalm 91: The Secret Place of the Most High
chapters.summary: Divine shelter under heavenly wings and deliverance from snare and pestilence.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Psalm 91:1-5, 11-12: Kaphāmei Kazingwui pamkaphunli pamkakhui chinana Pangashan Kapeiwui ngaching tharili pamsara. I Prohowui vang hangsara: 'A iwui rungkahai pam, iwui lungkhor kashang, iwui Varivara; Ali I chotkhangashit khuisara.' Ana vanaokhamakhui khangashun eina kala kasham kashikaza eina nali huikhuira. Ana Awui theirei eina nali kuplupsara, kala Awui phana ngashingli na rungpamsara: Awui mashung-tui nawui dhal kala kot thada kasaye.
chapters.english_translation: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust. Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence. He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
grammar_notes: Defensive weaponry metaphors in Tangkhul: 'dhal' (shield) and 'kot' (buckler/armor).
Metaphorical shelter using avian wing terminology: 'phana'.
exercises: Identify the titles for God in Psalm 91:1-2.
Translate verse 4 into modern Ukhrul idiom.

chapters.title: Psalm 121: The Traveler's Mountain Psalm (Kaphungli Yanglu)
chapters.summary: Lifting eyes to the hills from whence cometh help; the keeper who never slumbers.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Psalm 121:1-8: I iwui mik kaphung kashangli thuk-kashok-e: iwui khangachon kachikhali shokhungra? Iwui khangachon kazing kala ngalei sakahai Prohowui eina shokhunge! Ana nawui kakhutli ngasotkazip makasara: nali ngashankashapana mangaphama-mana! Theilu, Israel-li ngashankashapana mangaphama-mana, mapila-mana. Prohona nawui ngashankashapana; Prohona nawui kashikli nawui ngaching katha leisaye. Zingsho eina zingkhamathānna nali makara, ngazing eina kachanna nali mamakhura. Prohona nali kashikashili huikhuira: Ana nawui mangazingli ngashansara.
chapters.english_translation: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth. He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber. Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand. The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night. The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.
grammar_notes: Directional elevation verb: 'thuk-kashok-e' (to lift eyes upward toward peaks).
Paired physiological verbs of resting: 'mangaphama-mana, mapila-mana' (slumber not, sleep not).
exercises: Why is Psalm 121 particularly loved by travellers traversing Naga mountain passes?
Identify the celestial bodies contrasted in verse 6.

chapters.title: Psalm 150: The Grand Doxology with Traditional Instruments
chapters.summary: Praise the Lord with trumpet, harp, strings, dance, and clashing cymbals.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Psalm 150:1-6: Proholi mathat-eina kashaklu! Awui kathara shillongli Varivarali mathatlu! Awui pangashankazingli Ali mathatlu! Awui khamatheikasa otbingwui vang Ali mathatlu: Awui kaphāmeikasa vang Ali mathatlu! Torot (trumpet) kakhong eina Ali mathatlu: Harp kala Luishat-thing (lyre) eina Ali mathatlu! Tingteila (tambourine) kala pheichak (dance) eina Ali mathatlu: Tui-thingkhanghui (stringed organs) kala Pung (pipes) eina Ali mathatlu! Meikakhong chot eina Ali mathatlu: Khongyui kapei khong eina Ali mathatlu! Ringkashap kapeina Proholi mathat-eina kashaklu! Hallelujah!
chapters.english_translation: Praise ye the LORD. Praise God in his sanctuary: praise him in the firmament of his power. Praise him for his mighty acts: praise him according to his excellent greatness. Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals. Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.

vocabulary.meaning: bamboo pipe, flutes, musical wind organ

grammar_notes: Tangkhul traditional organology: 'pheichak' (dance), 'Pung' (pipes), 'tingteila' (traditional tambourine).
Repeated cohortative imperative: 'Ali mathatlu!' (Praise Him!).
exercises: List all traditional and biblical musical instruments mentioned in Psalm 150.
Explain the meaning of 'ringkashap kapei' (everything with breath).

pages.title: Psalm 91: The Secret Place of the Most High
lines: CHAPTER 3: PSALM 91: THE SECRET PLACE OF THE MOST HIGH
Summary: Divine shelter under heavenly wings and deliverance from snare and pestilence....
Psalm 91:1-5, 11-12: Kaphāmei Kazingwui pamkaphunli pamkakhui chinana
Pangashan Kapeiwui ngaching tharili pamsara. I Prohowui vang hangsara:
'A iwui rungkahai pam, iwui lungkhor kashang, iwui Varivara; Ali I
chotkhangashit khuisara.' Ana vanaokhamakhui khangashun eina kala kasham
kashikaza eina nali huikhuira. Ana Awui theirei eina nali kuplupsara,
kala Awui phana ngashingli na rungpamsara: Awui mashung-tui nawui dhal
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under
the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and
my fortress: my God; in him will I trust. Surely he shall deliver thee
from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence. He shall
cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his
truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
pages.tangkhul_content: Psalm 91:1-5, 11-12: Kaphāmei Kazingwui pamkaphunli pamkakhui chinana Pangashan Kapeiwui ngaching tharili pamsara. I Prohowui vang hangsara: 'A iwui rungkahai pam, iwui lungkhor kashang, iwui Varivara; Ali I chotkhangashit khuisara.' Ana vanaokhamakhui khangashun eina kala kasham kashikaza eina nali huikhuira. Ana Awui theirei eina nali kuplupsara, kala Awui phana ngashingli na rungpamsara: Awui mashung-tui nawui dhal kala kot thada kasaye.
pages.english_translation: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty. I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust. Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence. He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.

pages.title: Psalm 121: The Traveler's Mountain Psalm (Kaphungli Yanglu)
lines: CHAPTER 4: PSALM 121: THE TRAVELER'S MOUNTAIN PSALM (KAPHUNGLI YANGLU)
Summary: Lifting eyes to the hills from whence cometh help; the keeper who never slumbers...
Psalm 121:1-8: I iwui mik kaphung kashangli thuk-kashok-e: iwui
khangachon kachikhali shokhungra? Iwui khangachon kazing kala ngalei
sakahai Prohowui eina shokhunge! Ana nawui kakhutli ngasotkazip
makasara: nali ngashankashapana mangaphama-mana! Theilu, Israel-li
ngashankashapana; Prohona nawui kashikli nawui ngaching katha leisaye.
Zingsho eina zingkhamathānna nali makara, ngazing eina kachanna nali
mamakhura. Prohona nali kashikashili huikhuira: Ana nawui mangazingli
I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My
help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth. He will not
suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber.
Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. The LORD
is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand. The sun shall
not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night. The LORD shall preserve
thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.
pages.tangkhul_content: Psalm 121:1-8: I iwui mik kaphung kashangli thuk-kashok-e: iwui khangachon kachikhali shokhungra? Iwui khangachon kazing kala ngalei sakahai Prohowui eina shokhunge! Ana nawui kakhutli ngasotkazip makasara: nali ngashankashapana mangaphama-mana! Theilu, Israel-li ngashankashapana mangaphama-mana, mapila-mana. Prohona nawui ngashankashapana; Prohona nawui kashikli nawui ngaching katha leisaye. Zingsho eina zingkhamathānna nali makara, ngazing eina kachanna nali mamakhura. Prohona nali kashikashili huikhuira: Ana nawui mangazingli ngashansara.
pages.english_translation: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth. He will not suffer thy foot to be moved: he that keepeth thee will not slumber. Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep. The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand. The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night. The LORD shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.

pages.title: Psalm 150: The Grand Doxology with Traditional Instruments
lines: CHAPTER 5: PSALM 150: THE GRAND DOXOLOGY WITH TRADITIONAL INSTRUMENTS
Summary: Praise the Lord with trumpet, harp, strings, dance, and clashing cymbals....
Psalm 150:1-6: Proholi mathat-eina kashaklu! Awui kathara shillongli
Varivarali mathatlu! Awui pangashankazingli Ali mathatlu! Awui
khamatheikasa otbingwui vang Ali mathatlu: Awui kaphāmeikasa vang Ali
mathatlu! Torot (trumpet) kakhong eina Ali mathatlu: Harp kala Luishat-
thing (lyre) eina Ali mathatlu! Tingteila (tambourine) kala pheichak
(dance) eina Ali mathatlu: Tui-thingkhanghui (stringed organs) kala Pung
(pipes) eina Ali mathatlu! Meikakhong chot eina Ali mathatlu: Khongyui
kapei khong eina Ali mathatlu! Ringkashap kapeina Proholi mathat-eina
Praise ye the LORD. Praise God in his sanctuary: praise him in the
firmament of his power. Praise him for his mighty acts: praise him
according to his excellent greatness. Praise him with the sound of the
trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the
timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs.
Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding
cymbals. Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the

pages.english_translation: Praise ye the LORD. Praise God in his sanctuary: praise him in the firmament of his power. Praise him for his mighty acts: praise him according to his excellent greatness. Praise him with the sound of the trumpet: praise him with the psaltery and harp. Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals. Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.

title: Khangayeiwui Khayang: John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress in Tangkhul Naga
alternate_titles: The Pilgrim's Progress in Tangkhul Naga
publisher: Ukhrul Mission Press / Tangkhul Literature Society
subject: Allegorical Literature & World Classics Translated
notes: Historic Tangkhul translation of John Bunyan's immortal allegory The Pilgrim's Progress. Depicts Christian's journey from the City of Destruction (Kasham Shillong) to the Celestial City.

front_matter.title_page: Khangayeiwui Khayang: John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress in Tangkhul Naga (1932)
front_matter.preface: John Bunyan's 1678 allegory was rendered into Tangkhul Naga in the early 1930s. The allegory resonated profoundly with Tangkhul storytelling traditions: perilous mountain passes, giants, bogs of despondency, and fortified spiritual gates. It became one of the most widely read prose texts in Ukhrul and the surrounding hills.

chapters.title: The Burdened Pilgrim & Departure from the City of Destruction
chapters.summary: Christian weeping over his heavy burden, reading the Book, and Evangelist pointing to the Wicket Gate.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 1: I kachak ngaleili ramkhangateili yanglakha, kasham shillongli mayarnaowon akha theitserie. Awui pakhonli phashan kashang akha phunkahaye, kala awui khutli Lairik akha huikahaye. Ana Lairik chi hanglaga ngachire, kala 'I khipa sara? I katha eina huikhuira?' hoda chirkhangahok eina hohe. Chitharan Evangelist kaho mi akha awui ngalemli rarlaga hang: 'Nawui mik-ngalemli khong kakat chi theimacho?' Mayarnaowon china hang: 'Thei-mashuk-mana.' Evangelistna hang: 'Chitharan mangashan kashang chi theilu, kala chichi shurva-lu; chitharan na khong chithuili zanglaga huikhuira!'
chapters.english_translation: As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep: and as I slept, I dreamed a dream. I looked, and saw a man clothed with rags, standing in a certain place, with his face from his own house, a book in his hand, and a great burden upon his back. He wept and trembled; and not being able longer to contain, he brake out with a lamentable cry, saying, What shall I do? Then said Evangelist, pointing with his finger over a very wide field, Do you see yonder wicket-gate? The man said, No. Then said the other, Do you see yonder shining light? Keep that light in your eye, and go up directly thereto: so shalt thou see the gate.
grammar_notes: Tangkhul framing for dream vision: 'I kachak ngaleili... yanglakha' (As I surveyed in the world of dreams).
Emotional burst expression: 'chirkhangahok eina' (with weeping lamentation).
exercises: Identify the Tangkhul equivalent for 'Wicket Gate'.
Explain the psychological significance of the burden on the pilgrim's back.

chapters.title: The Slough of Despond & The Wicket Gate
chapters.summary: Christian sinks in the mire of despondency, is rescued by Help, and reaches the Strait Gate.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 2: Athum khani shongfa eina zatlakha, khamathān ngalung kashilashi kacham akhali tuisangserie; chiwui ming Despond Miram (Slough of Despond) hose. Chitharan Christianna awui pakhon kashang chiwui vang ngalungli ngashumsangie. Kha theilu, Help kaho mi akha rarlaga awui khutli huitsangserie, kala hang: 'Khikha mangachek-alu, shongfa mashungli rarlu!' Chiwui tharan Christianna khong kakatli vashuklaga kakorrie; kala Goodwillna khong hungkahanglaga ali shimsangie.
chapters.english_translation: They drew near to a very miry slough, that was in the midst of the plain; and they being heedless, did both fall suddenly into the bog. The name of the slough was Despond. Here therefore they wallowed for a time, being grievously bedaubed with dirt; and Christian, because of the burden that was on his back, began to sink in the mire. Then came a man to him whose name was Help, and said, Give me thine hand: so he gave him his hand, and he drew him out, and set him upon sound ground. Then Christian came up to the gate, and knocked, and Goodwill opened unto him.
grammar_notes: Idiomatic sink verb: 'ngashumsang' (to sink deeply into muddy morass).
Sequential narrative suffix '-laga': 'vashuklaga kakorrie' (having arrived, he knocked).
exercises: Contrast the characters Pliable and Christian in the Slough of Despond.
How is 'Help' represented in Tangkhul?

chapters.title: The Hill Difficulty & The Palace Beautiful
chapters.summary: Climbing the steep precipice of Difficulty, resting in the arbor, and arriving at the haven Palace Beautiful.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 3: Christianna Hill Difficulty kaho kaphung kashangli vashukrie. Shongfa chinawui chishatna kaphung kathara thada vaye, kala ana kakhut eina, khut eina kakhorlaga thuk-kashok-e. Kaphung wui ngalemli ana Shim Kaphā (Palace Beautiful) theitserie; kala chithuili Prudence, Piety, kala Charity kaho ngalanaobingna ali mathat-eina shimlaga kachak kaphā shaksakserie, kala khangaraorapwui thingkot chitheitserie.
chapters.english_translation: I looked then after Christian, to see him go up the hill, where I perceived he fell from running to going, and from going to clambering upon his hands and his knees, because of the steepness of the place. Then he came to the house called Beautiful; and the porter Watchful called Discretion, Piety, Prudence, and Charity, who welcomed him in, and gave him refreshment, and showed him the armory of celestial weapons.
grammar_notes: Progressive velocity transition: running -> walking -> crawling expressed with serial verb compounds.
Allegorical personification of Christian virtues in Tangkhul.
exercises: Translate 'clambering on hands and knees' into colloquial Tangkhul.
What virtues welcome Christian into Palace Beautiful?

chapters.title: The Valley of Humiliation & Conflict with Apollyon
chapters.summary: Descent into the valley, dread confrontation with Apollyon, and victory with the Sword of Truth.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 4: Christianna Longkhor Kakat (Valley of Humiliation) li zangsangie. Chitharan theilu, Apollyon kaho kasham sha akha rarlaga awui shongfali ngaphamsai. Awui aphasa meikashe katha, kala meikazat awui khong eina shoke. Ana Christianli hang: 'Nawui ramli valoo, na iwui mayarnao-sai!' Kha Christianna hang: 'I Kazingramwui Shiyankasangwui mayarnao-sai!' Apollyonna meithei shuklaga Christianli haksangie; kha Christianna awui sword eina Apollyonli kashukserie, kala Apollyonna phana pholaga ngakaphirserie!
chapters.english_translation: Now, in this Valley of Humiliation, poor Christian was hard put to it; for he had gone but a little way, before he espied a foul fiend coming over the field to meet him; his name is Apollyon. He was clothed with scales, and out of his belly came fire and smoke. Apollyon said, Thou hast done this according to the proverb, Change a bad for a worse: but there is no prince that will thus lightly lose his subjects, neither will I as yet lose thee: return. Christian answered, I am the servant of the King of princes! Then did Christian nimbly stretch out his hand for his sword, and caught it, saying, Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise. And with that he gave him a deadly thrust, and Apollyon spread forth his dragon's wings, and sped him away.

vocabulary.meaning: Sovereign King of Kings, High Lord
fled rapidly, flew away in defeat

grammar_notes: Adversarial encounter narrative discourse.
Tangkhul dragon/beast terminology: 'meikashe katha' (scaled like a serpent/pangolin).
exercises: Describe Apollyon using the Tangkhul descriptive phrases.
How did Christian overcome the adversary?

chapters.title: Vanity Fair & The Celestial City (Jerusalem Kathara)
chapters.summary: Faithful's martyrdom at Vanity Fair, Christian reaching the River of Death, and entry into Celestial Glory.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 5: Christian kala Faithfulna Vanity Fair kaho phanit kashangli vashukrie, chithuili mikumona ngaleiwui saphā-kashang kazip-kasaye. Faithfulna kashung tui hangkaji vang chithuili thiri; kha ana kazingramwui chariot eina chithangathukserie. Christianna Hopeful eina zanglaga River of Deathli vashukrie; kala kapei tui katek-tek ngakorlaga athum kazingramwui Shillong Katharali vashukserie! Chitharan athumli kachon kachak sangmi, kala shillong tharili trumpet khongrie: 'Rarlu, ithui Shiyankasangwui mathatli zanglu!' Kala i khangayangli ngakhur-rarlakna.
chapters.english_translation: Then I saw in my dream, that they went on, until they came into a fair, called Vanity Fair, where all kinds of worldly wares are sold. Faithful was condemned and put to death, but a chariot waited to take him through the clouds into the Celestial City. Christian and Hopeful came to the River without a bridge, and passing through the deep waters, they arrived at the Mount Zion. The Shining Ones welcomed them: Enter ye into the joy of your Lord. And all the bells in the city rang again for joy; and lo, it was a dream, and I awoke.

vocabulary.meaning: awoke from dream vision, opened eyes

grammar_notes: Dream-vision awakening frame: 'kala i khangayangli ngakhur-rarlakna' (and lo, I awoke).
Contrast between 'ngaleiwui saphā' (worldly riches) and 'kazingramwui mathat' (heavenly joy).
exercises: Explain the moral message of Vanity Fair in Bunyan's allegory.
Translate the closing dream awakening sentence into Tangkhul.

pages.title: Preface by the Translators
lines: John Bunyan's 1678 allegory was rendered into Tangkhul Naga in the early
1930s. The allegory resonated profoundly with Tangkhul storytelling
traditions: perilous mountain passes, giants, bogs of despondency, and
fortified spiritual gates. It became one of the most widely read prose
texts in Ukhrul and the surrounding hills.

pages.title: The Burdened Pilgrim & Departure from the City of Destruction
lines: CHAPTER 1: THE BURDENED PILGRIM & DEPARTURE FROM THE CITY OF DESTRUCTION
Summary: Christian weeping over his heavy burden, reading the Book, and Evangelist pointi...
Chapter 1: I kachak ngaleili ramkhangateili yanglakha, kasham shillongli
mayarnaowon akha theitserie. Awui pakhonli phashan kashang akha
phunkahaye, kala awui khutli Lairik akha huikahaye. Ana Lairik chi
hanglaga ngachire, kala 'I khipa sara? I katha eina huikhuira?' hoda
chirkhangahok eina hohe. Chitharan Evangelist kaho mi akha awui ngalemli
rarlaga hang: 'Nawui mik-ngalemli khong kakat chi theimacho?'
'Chitharan mangashan kashang chi theilu, kala chichi shurva-lu;
chitharan na khong chithuili zanglaga huikhuira!'
As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain
place where was a den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep: and as
I slept, I dreamed a dream. I looked, and saw a man clothed with rags,
standing in a certain place, with his face from his own house, a book in
his hand, and a great burden upon his back. He wept and trembled; and
not being able longer to contain, he brake out with a lamentable cry,
saying, What shall I do? Then said Evangelist, pointing with his finger
over a very wide field, Do you see yonder wicket-gate? The man said, No.
Then said the other, Do you see yonder shining light? Keep that light in
your eye, and go up directly thereto: so shalt thou see the gate.

Summary: Christian sinks in the mire of despondency, is rescued by Help, and reaches the ...

mashungli rarlu!' Chiwui tharan Christianna khong kakatli vashuklaga
kakorrie; kala Goodwillna khong hungkahanglaga ali shimsangie.

his hand, and he drew him out, and set him upon sound ground. Then

pages.english_translation: They drew near to a very miry slough, that was in the midst of the plain; and they being heedless, did both fall suddenly into the bog. The name of the slough was Despond. Here therefore they wallowed for a time, being grievously bedaubed with dirt; and Christian, because of the burden that was on his back, began to sink in the mire. Then came a man to him whose name was Help, and said, Give me thine hand: so he gave him his hand, and he drew him out, and set him upon sound ground. Then Christian came up to the gate, and knocked, and Goodwill opened unto him.

pages.title: The Valley of Humiliation & Conflict with Apollyon
lines: CHAPTER 4: THE VALLEY OF HUMILIATION & CONFLICT WITH APOLLYON
Summary: Descent into the valley, dread confrontation with Apollyon, and victory with the...
Chapter 4: Christianna Longkhor Kakat (Valley of Humiliation) li
zangsangie. Chitharan theilu, Apollyon kaho kasham sha akha rarlaga awui
shongfali ngaphamsai. Awui aphasa meikashe katha, kala meikazat awui
khong eina shoke. Ana Christianli hang: 'Nawui ramli valoo, na iwui
mayarnao-sai!' Kha Christianna hang: 'I Kazingramwui Shiyankasangwui
mayarnao-sai!' Apollyonna meithei shuklaga Christianli haksangie; kha
Christianna awui sword eina Apollyonli kashukserie, kala Apollyonna
Now, in this Valley of Humiliation, poor Christian was hard put to it;
for he had gone but a little way, before he espied a foul fiend coming
over the field to meet him; his name is Apollyon. He was clothed with
scales, and out of his belly came fire and smoke. Apollyon said, Thou
hast done this according to the proverb, Change a bad for a worse: but
there is no prince that will thus lightly lose his subjects, neither
will I as yet lose thee: return. Christian answered, I am the servant of
the King of princes! Then did Christian nimbly stretch out his hand for
his sword, and caught it, saying, Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy:
when I fall, I shall arise. And with that he gave him a deadly thrust,
and Apollyon spread forth his dragon's wings, and sped him away.
pages.tangkhul_content: Chapter 4: Christianna Longkhor Kakat (Valley of Humiliation) li zangsangie. Chitharan theilu, Apollyon kaho kasham sha akha rarlaga awui shongfali ngaphamsai. Awui aphasa meikashe katha, kala meikazat awui khong eina shoke. Ana Christianli hang: 'Nawui ramli valoo, na iwui mayarnao-sai!' Kha Christianna hang: 'I Kazingramwui Shiyankasangwui mayarnao-sai!' Apollyonna meithei shuklaga Christianli haksangie; kha Christianna awui sword eina Apollyonli kashukserie, kala Apollyonna phana pholaga ngakaphirserie!

pages.title: Vanity Fair & The Celestial City (Jerusalem Kathara)
lines: CHAPTER 5: VANITY FAIR & THE CELESTIAL CITY (JERUSALEM KATHARA)
Summary: Faithful's martyrdom at Vanity Fair, Christian reaching the River of Death, and ...
Chapter 5: Christian kala Faithfulna Vanity Fair kaho phanit kashangli
vashukrie, chithuili mikumona ngaleiwui saphā-kashang kazip-kasaye.
Faithfulna kashung tui hangkaji vang chithuili thiri; kha ana
kazingramwui chariot eina chithangathukserie. Christianna Hopeful eina
zanglaga River of Deathli vashukrie; kala kapei tui katek-tek ngakorlaga
athum kazingramwui Shillong Katharali vashukserie! Chitharan athumli
kachon kachak sangmi, kala shillong tharili trumpet khongrie: 'Rarlu,
ithui Shiyankasangwui mathatli zanglu!' Kala i khangayangli ngakhur-
Then I saw in my dream, that they went on, until they came into a fair,
called Vanity Fair, where all kinds of worldly wares are sold. Faithful
was condemned and put to death, but a chariot waited to take him through
the clouds into the Celestial City. Christian and Hopeful came to the
River without a bridge, and passing through the deep waters, they
arrived at the Mount Zion. The Shining Ones welcomed them: Enter ye into
the joy of your Lord. And all the bells in the city rang again for joy;
and lo, it was a dream, and I awoke.
pages.tangkhul_content: Chapter 5: Christian kala Faithfulna Vanity Fair kaho phanit kashangli vashukrie, chithuili mikumona ngaleiwui saphā-kashang kazip-kasaye. Faithfulna kashung tui hangkaji vang chithuili thiri; kha ana kazingramwui chariot eina chithangathukserie. Christianna Hopeful eina zanglaga River of Deathli vashukrie; kala kapei tui katek-tek ngakorlaga athum kazingramwui Shillong Katharali vashukserie! Chitharan athumli kachon kachak sangmi, kala shillong tharili trumpet khongrie: 'Rarlu, ithui Shiyankasangwui mathatli zanglu!' Kala i khangayangli ngakhur-rarlakna.
pages.english_translation: Then I saw in my dream, that they went on, until they came into a fair, called Vanity Fair, where all kinds of worldly wares are sold. Faithful was condemned and put to death, but a chariot waited to take him through the clouds into the Celestial City. Christian and Hopeful came to the River without a bridge, and passing through the deep waters, they arrived at the Mount Zion. The Shining Ones welcomed them: Enter ye into the joy of your Lord. And all the bells in the city rang again for joy; and lo, it was a dream, and I awoke.

title: Aesopwui Khararchan: Translated Aesop's Fables & Moral Stories in Tangkhul
alternate_titles: Aesop's Fables Translated into Tangkhul Naga
subject: Fables, Children Literature & Moral Instruction
notes: Classic translation of Aesop's Fables into Tangkhul Naga by TLS. Includes beloved timeless animal allegories adapted with native flora, fauna, and idioms of the Tangkhul hills.

front_matter.title_page: Aesopwui Khararchan: Translated Aesop's Fables & Moral Stories in Tangkhul (1978)
front_matter.preface: The translation of Aesop's Fables by the Tangkhul Literature Society provided generation after generation of Tangkhul school children with lively didactic stories. The translator ingeniously mapped Aesop's animals to familiar Himalayan highland counterparts: the hare became 'ngachon', the tortoise 'shimhar', the wolf 'ngayen', and the fox 'sharu', preserving the universal moral truth of each fable.

chapters.summary: The boastful hare challenged by the slow but persevering tortoise in Tangkhul prose.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 1: Thot akha ngachon kashap akha leisai. Ana kashikatha sha pupupli 'I thada khangachon pamei malei!' hoda aphasa mathaikhangasang leisai. Chitharan shimhar kacham akha rarlaga hang: 'Ngachon, na eina i race khaksa-u!' Ngachonna mania: 'Na thada kachut-kachut zatnao china ili khaksa-ra kaji?' Kha athum race phokserie. Ngachonna shongzali khangachon thotlaga 'Shimhar kashapli kachut; i thingphun ngachingli ngaphama-u' hoda pilakna. Kha shimharna kakhut machamla zatpingsanglaga, goal line-li khare vashukrie! Moral (Tuitam): Ningkazang eina chotkasana khangaraorap khuiye.
chapters.english_translation: A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow. 'Do you ever get anywhere?' he asked with a mocking laugh. 'Yes,' replied the Tortoise, 'and I get there sooner than you think. Run with me and I will prove it.' The Hare was much amused at the idea of running a race with the Tortoise, but for the fun of the thing he agreed. The Hare was soon far out of sight, and to make the Tortoise appear very ridiculous, he lay down beside the course to take a nap until the Tortoise should catch up. The Tortoise meanwhile kept going slowly but steadily, and, after a time, passed the place where the Hare was sleeping. When the Hare awoke, the Tortoise was across the finish line! Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
grammar_notes: Reduplicated manner adverb: 'kachut-kachut' (slowly and methodically).
Moral summary particle: 'Tuitam' (teaching/moral lesson).
exercises: Summarize the story of the Tortoise and the Hare in three Tangkhul sentences.
Translate the moral 'Slow and steady wins the race' into Tangkhul.

chapters.title: Sharu kala Sakalu (The Fox and the Grapes)
chapters.summary: The cunning fox leaping for sweet grapes and declaring them sour when out of reach.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 2: Sharu akha kachak kashaklaga ramkhangateili zatlakha, thingphunli shantuk-kahai sakalu (grapes) theitserie. Sakalu chi thik-thik kacha, chithei kaphā kala tui-ngapom kachuk theilaga sharu chi shashik thotna. Ana sakalu khukhavai kaphungli thuksange; kha vashuk mashuk-mana. Khani, kathum chuksa-ngasotlakha khikha phā mashuk-mana. Chitharan sharuna awui makhayor mathatlaga hang: 'Khai! Sakalu hi kakhui-kashasai! Ili kakhui thei shakkhavai ning maleimana!' hoda valakna. Moral (Tuitam): Phā-mashuk-khalangli kashikahai hoda hangkasa mi kachungsai.
chapters.english_translation: A famished Fox will tell you, if he can, of the sweet grapes that hung from a vine high on a trellis. He longed to reach them, but they were beyond his leap. He took a running start and jumped, but missed. Again and again he tried after the tempting morsel, but at last had to give it up. He walked off with his nose in the air, saying: 'I thought those grapes were ripe, but I see now they are quite sour.' Moral: It is easy to despise what you cannot get.
grammar_notes: Verbal attempt compound: 'chuksa-ngasotlakha' (having tried jumping repeatedly).
Compound adjective for taste: 'kakhui' (bitter/tart) + 'kasha' (sour).
exercises: What rationalization did the fox offer for walking away?
Identify the Tangkhul words for leaping and failing to reach.

chapters.title: Avaikha kacham ngalanao kala Ngayen (The Boy Who Cried Wolf)
chapters.summary: The young shepherd crying wolf falsely and finding no one believes a liar even when telling the truth.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 3: Mayarnaowon akhana kaphungli avaikha (sheep) kashun leisai. Ana shongfa khangayeili ngacham-kaza chiwui vang khanganoilaga hohe: 'Ngayen! Ngayen rarlakna! Avaikha shaksangie!' Village-wui mikumo thapup thingkot khuilaga khangachonli rarer; kha chithuili ngayen malei-mana, mayarnaowon china kanganrilaga pamye. Zingkum khani hithada saserie. Chitharan zingsho akha kashung-mashung ngayen rarlakna! Mayarnaowon china lungkashung eina hohe: 'Ngayen rarlakna! Khangachon milu!' Kha mikumo akhakhana mashursang-mana, 'A maningkachang tui hangye' hoda leisai. Chitharan ngayenna avaikha pupupli shaksangserie. Moral (Tuitam): Maningkachang mi kashung tui hangkhalangli khipana machotsang-mana.
chapters.english_translation: There was once a young Shepherd Boy who tended his sheep at the foot of a mountain near a dark forest. It was rather lonely for him, so he thought upon a plan by which he could get a little company and some excitement. He rushed down towards the village calling out 'Wolf, Wolf,' and the villagers came out to help him. He laughed at them when they found no wolf. This he did twice. At last, a real Wolf came out from the forest. The boy cried in earnest terror, 'Wolf, Wolf, please come!' But the villagers thought he was deceiving them again, and nobody came to his aid. Moral: Nobody believes a liar, even when he tells the truth.
grammar_notes: Deceptive speech classifier: 'maningkachang tui' (untrue words/lies).
Temporal iterative: 'zingkum khani hithada saserie' (did so two or three times).
exercises: Discuss the social consequences of falsehood in traditional village governance.
Translate the moral lesson into Hindi and English.

chapters.title: Samayār kala Khachangnao (The Lion and the Mouse)
chapters.summary: The mighty lion sparing the tiny mouse, who later gnaws the hunter's ropes to free the king of beasts.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 4: Samayār (lion) kashang akha thingphun ngachingli ngaphamsai. Khachangnao (mouse) kacham akhana awui mai-ngalungli ngachonkatlakha, samayārna awui khut eina khuikahaisai. Khachangnaona khamathān haikaphā salaga hang: 'Shiyankasang, ili huikhuilu! Thot akha i nawui khangachon sarap sara!' Samayārna kanganrilaga ali kashikahaiserie. Zingsho charakha ngaphalaga, hunterbingna samayārli rui kashang eina thuksangie. Samayārna khongyui eina hu-hu kashoklakha, khachangnaona rarlaga awui khani-eina rui chi kakor-khakserie! Samayār chi ngatorie. Moral (Tuitam): Kakatnaobingna kashangbingli khangachon sara kashap lei.
chapters.english_translation: A Lion was awakened by a Mouse running over his face. Rising in angry wrath, he laid his paw upon him with intent to kill him. The Mouse piteously entreated him: 'Spare me, O King! and I will surely repay your kindness.' The Lion laughed and let him go. Some time after, the Lion was caught in the net of the hunters. He roared with fury. The Mouse recognized his roar, ran to the net, and gnawed the ropes with his teeth until he set the king free. Moral: Little friends may prove great friends.
grammar_notes: Tangkhul rodent gnawing verb: 'kakor-khak' (to sever completely by gnawing).
Diminutive suffix '-nao' marking smallness/humility (khachangnao = tiny mouse).
exercises: Contrast the physical sizes and reciprocal deeds of the lion and the mouse.
How does Tangkhul grammar express unexpected assistance?

pages.title: Preface by the Translators
lines: The translation of Aesop's Fables by the Tangkhul Literature Society
provided generation after generation of Tangkhul school children with
lively didactic stories. The translator ingeniously mapped Aesop's
animals to familiar Himalayan highland counterparts: the hare became
'ngachon', the tortoise 'shimhar', the wolf 'ngayen', and the fox
'sharu', preserving the universal moral truth of each fable.

chapters.title: Gitanjali Song 1: Thou Hast Made Me Endless (Na Ili Machamtui Sakahaisaye)
chapters.summary: Tagore's opening offering: the human soul as a frail flute through which God breathes eternal melodies.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Shai-laa 1: Na ili machamtui sakahaisaye, chichi Nawui ningkazangsai. Hi kacham kaphunga vessel hi Na khani-kathum khangareilaga kupsang-miye, kala zingsho zingsho ringkapha kathara eina kashung-sake. Hi kakat bamboo reed flute hi Na kaphung-longkhor kuppupli phungzatlaga, Awui ngalung eina thot pupupwui shai-laaring honsangserie. Nawui kathara khutwui katom eina iwui kacham lung china khangayeiwui mathatli ngapaoritlaga khongyui kapei honsange.
chapters.english_translation: Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life. This little flute of a reed thou hast carried over hills and dales, and hast breathed through it melodies eternally new. At the immortal touch of thy hands my little heart loses its limits in joy and gives birth to utterance ineffable.

vocabulary.meaning: Siphung / Pung (bamboo flute of the hills)
gentle touch, caress of divine hand

grammar_notes: Metaphorical transposition: Tagore's reed flute rendered as traditional Tangkhul 'siphung'.
Verbal frequentative: 'khani-kathum khangareilaga' (emptying repeatedly again and again).
exercises: Discuss how the flute metaphor bridges Bengali Vaishnava mysticism and Tangkhul music.
Identify the words for 'endless' and 'immortal touch'.

chapters.title: Where the Mind is Without Fear (Mangmatha Mathikhavai Ram)
chapters.summary: Tagore's universal prayer for freedom, truth, and unconstrained intellectual dignity in Tangkhul verse.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Shai-laa 35: Kachikhali ningkakhaning malei-mana, kala kakhutli phashan eina thuk-kashok-e; Kachikhali theikakhui chi mikumo pupupwui vang kacham eina ngashankahaye; Kachikhali ngalei hi shimwui wall kakat eina kashit-mashit-mana; Kachikhali tui-ngashungna lungwui kashikli eina shokhunge; Kachikhali khangachonna khut machamla phāmeikhavai otli thukzat-e; Kachikhali mashung-ngalungwui kongkhamathān china kasham custom-wui miram kashilashili mangapaorit-mana; Chithuili, I-Ava, Nawui khut eina iwui ramli ngakhur-rarsaklu!
chapters.english_translation: Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls; Where words come out from the depth of truth; Where tireless striving stretches its arms towards perfection; Where the clear stream of reason has not lost its way into the dreary desert sand of dead habit; Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake.
grammar_notes: Locative anaphora: 'Kachikhali... Kachikhali...' (Where... Where...).
Aspiration invocation: 'I-Ava, Nawui khut eina... ngakhur-rarsaklu!' (Father, let my nation awake!).
exercises: Recite 'Where the Mind is Without Fear' in Tangkhul.
How does the translator render 'narrow domestic walls'?

chapters.title: Leave This Chanting and Singing (Gitanjali Song 11)
chapters.summary: Finding God not in closed temples, but with the tiller of the soil and pathmaker breaking stones.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Shai-laa 11: Hi luishat-laa kala rosary chinawui khangayei kashikahailu! Shimkhur ngachingli khong kakat khangakhakli Na khipali reot-kasa? Nawui mik hanglu, kala theilu, Nawui Varivara chithuili maleimana! A tilling kasana luiramli ot salakha Awui ngalemli lei; A lungkhor khakka-sana shongfa shomlakha Awui ngalemli lei; A zingsho zingkhamathān kala kazingkhamik tharili athum eina li-leie, Awui chon ngaleiwui kachak eina kashung-saye. Nawui kathara chon kashikahailaga, A thada ngaleili varlu!
chapters.english_translation: Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee! He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones. He is with them in sun and in shower, and his garment is covered with dust. Put off thy holy mantle and even like him go down on the dusty soil!
grammar_notes: Agrarian elevation of labor: God resides with field tillers ('luiramli ot').
Imperative detachment: 'kashikahailu' (leave aside, abandon ritualism).
exercises: Compare Tagore's critique of ritualism with Tangkhul traditional values of honest physical labor.
Identify the words for sun and rain in verse 4.

chapters.title: Where Love Is, God Is (Khanganing kala Varivara) -- Leo Tolstoy
chapters.summary: Martin Avdeitch the cobbler looking for Christ and finding Him in the freezing stranger, hungry mother, and apple boy.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 1: Martin Avdeitch kaho shoemaker akhana khong-ngaching shimli pamsai. Ana zingsho pupup Lairik Kathara hanglaga ningkazang kazip-kasaye. Ngazing akha ana khongyui akhata kapeiye: 'Martin! Martin! Yanglu zingsho kashokli I nawui ngalemli rara!' Zingkhamathān shoklakha, Martinna window eina kashikathali yanglakha, Stepan kaho mayarnao kacham kashikaza akha snow ngalungli ngachek-kashung pamsai theitserie. Martinna ali shimsanglaga meikhangahui tharili tea kashak milaga chotkhangashit tui hangmi. Chitharan shanaowon akha awui naonli kachon maleilakha chirzat-lakha theilaga ali kachon kala paisa miye. Ngazing-tharan Martinna theitserie: 'Awui mai eina Christana hung-kachitheisaye: kasakei kachamnaobingli sakasashikahai ot pupup chi ili sakasashisaye!'
chapters.english_translation: In a little basement room in a certain city lived Martin Avdeitch, a cobbler. Every evening he read the Gospels until his heart burned within him. One night he heard a voice calling him: 'Martin, look out into the street tomorrow, for I will come.' Next day, while watching out the window, he saw Stepanitch clearing snow, shivering in rags; he called him in and gave him warm tea. Later he sheltered a poor mother with a child wrapped in thin garments and gave her his cloak and money. At dusk he realized: Christ had indeed visited him that day, for 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.'
grammar_notes: Direct quote attribution in Tangkhul narrative: 'hoda leisai' / 'hoda hang'.
Spiritual realization clause: 'Awui mai eina Christana hung-kachitheisaye'.
exercises: What three people did Martin encounter during the snowy day?
Explain the ethical message of Tolstoy's story.

chapters.title: The Necklace (Khangaphei wui Phasang) -- Guy de Maupassant
chapters.summary: Mathilde Loisel borrowing the diamond necklace, losing it at the ball, and toiling ten years for a tragic revelation.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 2: Mathilde Loisel kaho ngalashana kaphā akha pamsai; kha ana kashang-phā saphā-kashangli pamei lungkakhui leisai. Ministry-wui grand ball phanitli valakhavai ana awui ngalemwui Madame Forestier eina diamond necklace (phasang) khuiye. Ball phanitli mathat-eina pheichak salaga, shimli hung-kaphung tharan, theilu! Awui phasang chi ngashiman-serie! Mathilde kala awui va-na ten years kuppup kashakashi ot salaga 36,000 francs kashunsangserie phasang kathara khuisangkhavai. Kum thakharā ngaphalaga ana Madame Forestierli champsangie; chitharan Forestierna hang: 'Oh, Mathilde! Iwui phasang chi paste (artificial) sai! Awui value 500 francs kacham-sai!'
chapters.english_translation: Mathilde Loisel was a charming woman born into a family of clerks who dreamed of wealth and luxury. Invited to a grand ball at the Ministry, she borrowed a magnificent diamond necklace from her wealthy friend Madame Forestier. She was the belle of the ball, but arriving home, discovered to her horror that the necklace was lost. Rather than admit the loss, she and her husband worked ten grueling years in squalor and debt to purchase a replacement necklace for thirty-six thousand francs. Ten years later, meeting Madame Forestier in the park, aged and haggard, she learned the devastating truth: 'Oh my poor Mathilde! Mine was false! It was worth at most five hundred francs!'
grammar_notes: Tangkhul dramatic ironic reversal marker: 'theilu!' (Behold!).
French loanword handling: francs and ball phonetically adapted in Tangkhul narrative prose.
exercises: Describe Mathilde's character flaws and their consequences.
How does the story highlight the folly of excessive pride?

chapters.title: The Gift of the Magi (Magibingwui Khangashe) -- O. Henry
chapters.summary: Della selling her hair for a watch chain and Jim selling his watch for her hair combs in unconditional sacrificial love.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Khararchan 3: Della eina Jimna kacham shimli pamsai; Christmas tharili Della-li dollar 1.87 kacham leisai. Awui va Jimli Christmas gift mikhavai, ana awui kaphāmei sam (hair) pashitsanglaga Jimwui gold watch wui platinum chain khuiye. Ngazing-tharan Jimna shimli zanglaga Della-wui sam katat theilaga ngachekserie: kasakei Jimna awui gold watch pashitsanglaga Della-wui sam kaphā kachikhavai tortoise-shell combs khuisang-kahaisai! Athum khaniwui gift ngashiman thada theilashu, athumna magibing thada kaphāmei khangayei eina kashang thotna.
chapters.english_translation: One dollar and eighty-seven cents was all Della had on Christmas Eve to buy a present for her husband Jim. In sacrificial devotion, she sold her glorious cascading brown hair for twenty dollars to purchase a platinum fob chain for Jim's prized gold watch. When Jim returned home, he stared at her shorn hair in stunned amazement: for he had sold his gold watch to purchase the expensive set of tortoiseshell combs Della had long coveted! Though their material treasures were made temporarily useless, they were the wisest of all who give gifts--they were the Magi.

chapters.english_translation: WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

chapters.title: Fundamental Rights (Article 14 to 32)
chapters.summary: Rights to equality, freedom of speech, personal liberty, and constitutional remedies translated for Tangkhul citizens.
chapters.tangkhul_text:
Fundamental Rights (Hao Citizen Rights):
1. Article 14: Law-wui ngalemli mikumo pupup khangayam leisaye (Equality before law).
2. Article 19: Tui hangkhavai, phanit sakhavai, kala union kasakhavai mathat (Freedom of speech & assembly).
3. Article 21: Ringkapha kala personal liberty huikhuikhavai rights.
4. Article 25: Chotkhangashit kala reot-kasavai freedom.
5. Article 29-30: Minority language, script kala culture ngashankhavai rights.
6. Article 32: Supreme Court kala High Court-li writ petition eina rights huikhuikhavai remedies.
chapters.english_translation: Overview of Part III of the Constitution: Equality before the law, six freedoms of Article 19, protection of life and personal liberty under Article 21, freedom of religion under Article 25, minority cultural and linguistic protections under Articles 29-30, and the right to constitutional remedies under Article 32.
grammar_notes: Legal rights nomenclature: 'rights ngashankhavai' (safeguarding of rights).
Universal quantifier: 'mikumo pupup' (all citizens without exception).
exercises: Why are Articles 29 and 30 crucial for Tangkhul linguistic preservation?
Translate Article 21 into Tangkhul.

chapters.title: Customary Law, Village Courts (Hangva) & Article 371
chapters.summary: Integration of indigenous tribal customary law, village councils, and constitutional special autonomy provisions.
chapters.tangkhul_text:
Hao Ngashan kala Constitutional Protection:
Tangkhul village pupupli traditional council hoda Hangva (Village Court) leisaye. Awungshina headman hoda court-wui tui khak-kasaye. Article 371A kala 371C-wui provisions eina tribal customary laws, land ownership (ngalei khangayei), and civil justice-li constitutional autonomy miserie. Hangvawui decisions customary law eina sashung-khalang, formal law courtsna chichi respect salaga ngashane.
chapters.english_translation: Tribal customary governance operates through the Hangva (Village Council and Court) presided over by the Awungshi (village chief/headman). Constitutional provisions including Article 371 safeguard indigenous customary laws, land tenure systems, and traditional conflict resolution from arbitrary legislative interference.

title: Shimreishang kala Maitonphi: The Classic Tangkhul Epic Novel of Love and Tragedy
alternate_titles: Maitonphi eina Shimreishang: The Tangkhul Romeo and Juliet
The Legend of Star-Crossed Lovers in Ukhrul and Phadang
subject: Novel (Upanyas), Epic Romance & Traditional Tragedy
educational_level: Secondary, Higher Secondary & B.A. Tangkhul Literature
notes: The supreme classic novel of Tangkhul literature. Immortalizes the legendary romance between Shimreishang Zimikwo and Maitonphi Lungleng, torn apart by clan feuds, unyielding customary laws, and destiny.

front_matter.title_page: Shimreishang kala Maitonphi: The Classic Tangkhul Epic Novel of Love and Tragedy (1972)
front_matter.preface: Shimreishang kala Maitonphi stands as the undisputed crown jewel of Tangkhul imaginative prose literature. Comparable in cultural stature to Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet or Heer Ranjha of Punjab, this epic novel recounts the star-crossed love of Shimreishang, a valiant youth of the Zimikwo clan, and Maitonphi, the most graceful maiden of Phadang. It vividly portrays 18th-century Tangkhul village life, jhum farming rituals, village festivals, and the tragic conflict between individual romantic passion and immutable tribal customary codes.

chapters.title: The Spring Meeting at Luira Festival (Luira Phanitli Khangacham)
chapters.summary: Shimreishang and Maitonphi meet during the Hao Pheichak circle dance in the flowering hills.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 1: Zingyur atamli Luira Phanit shoklakha, Ukhrul ram kaphung-longkhor kuppup mathāteiye. Shimreishang, Zimikwo shangwui mayarnao kaphā, awui Haora chon eina pheichak shomye. Chitharan Maitonphi Lungleng, Phadang ramwui ngalanao kachak-ngayei, Luirim kachon sanglaga pheichak ngalungli ngaburleisai. Athum mik-ngalem khangacha tharan, Shimreishangwui lungli wonkhamathā pomsangie. Ana Awui shai-laaring honsangmi: 'Won kaphā, nali theilaga iwui lungkashungna nali ngashankahuie!'
chapters.english_translation: When the spring seed-sowing festival (Luira Phanit) arrived, all the hills and ravines of Ukhrul bloomed with celestial glory. Shimreishang, the gallant son of the Zimikwo clan, adorned his shoulders with the majestic Haora shawl to dance in the circle. There stood Maitonphi Lungleng, the radiant maiden of Phadang, wrapped in her graceful Luirim attire. When their gazes locked across the festive throng, a sacred flower of love blossomed in Shimreishang's heart. He sang his poetic lyric: 'O sweetest blossom, beholding thee, my whole heart surrenders in eternal devotion!'

vocabulary.meaning: spring season, time of vernal blooms
traditional black and red striped ceremonial male shawl
beautiful blossom of love, noble affection

grammar_notes: Seasonal temporal framing: 'Zingyur atamli... shoklakha' (When spring season arrived).
Poetic compounding: 'won' (flower) + 'khamathā' (beautiful) = flower of romance.
exercises: Describe the setting of Luira Phanit where the two lovers first meet.
Identify the traditional woven shawls worn by Shimreishang and Maitonphi.

chapters.title: The Secret Vow on Shirui Mountain (Shirui Kaphungli Tui-ngashik)
chapters.summary: Ascending the mystical heights of Shirui Kashong, the lovers pledge eternal faithfulness amid Kashong lilies.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 2: Athum khani Shirui Kashong kaphung kashangli thukzat-serie. Chithuili Shirui Lily won kaphā kachak eina ngasomleisai. Shimreishangna Maitonphili Shirui Lily akha shitsanglaga awui samli hamsangmi. Maitonphina mukthi kashik eina hang: 'Shimreishang, ithui shang khaniwui ngachaili kashan lei; ithui avava-na ithuli ngaror-kashap sara macho?' Shimreishangna awui khutli huitsanglaga tui-ngashik sakahaisai: 'Ngalei hi ngapaoritsashu, iwui khangayei nawui vang thot pupup mathimara!'
chapters.english_translation: The two climbed the sacred crest of Mount Shirui, where the unique pink Shirui Lilies bloomed in virgin purity. Shimreishang plucked a rare blossom and lovingly placed it in Maitonphi's dark hair. With tears glistening in her eyes, Maitonphi whispered: 'Shimreishang, an unyielding clan barrier divides our families; will our parents ever grant blessing to our union?' Grasping her hand firmly, Shimreishang swore an inviolable oath: 'Though heaven and earth may vanish away, my love for thee shall never perish throughout eternity!'

vocabulary.meaning: Mount Shirui, legendary peak of Ukhrul

grammar_notes: Highland botanical imagery: Shirui Lily as emblem of endangered romantic purity.
Irrevocable conditional oath formula: 'Ngalei hi ngapaoritsashu...' (Even if earth were to perish...).
exercises: Analyze the symbolic significance of Mount Shirui and the Shirui Lily in Tangkhul literature.
Translate Shimreishang's vow into Hindi and English.

chapters.title: Clan Feuds & The Forced Betrothal (Shangwui Kashan kala Kaphankahai)
chapters.summary: Inter-village clan hostilities erupt; Maitonphi's elders betroth her against her will to an elder chieftain.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 3: Ukhrul kala Phadangwui ngachaili ramkashikhavai tui-ngapom shokserie. Maitonphiwui avashimna ali Zimikwo shang eina khangayei sakhavai kakhamrie. Chiwui tharan kashang awungshi akha rarlaga Maitonphili marriage-wui vang bride-price (Man) mithukserie. Maitonphina zingsho ngazing kachikhali chirkhangahok eina Shimreishangli ningkhamathan leisai; kha customary law-wui khongyui kapei eina ana awui va-vawui tui mathakakhui mashuk-mana. Ana Shimreishangli pao-phungnao eina kashonmi: 'Iwui aphasa khangateili pashitsashu, iwui mangazing nawuisai!'
chapters.english_translation: Bitter clan rivalries erupted between the territories of Ukhrul and Phadang. Maitonphi's family strictly forbade any association with the Zimikwo lineage. Soon, an influential chieftain arrived and paid a heavy customary bride-price for Maitonphi's hand. Maitonphi wept day and night in inconsolable anguish, yearning for Shimreishang; yet bound by the iron edict of customary law, she could not disobey her elders. She sent a secret message: 'Though my physical body be bartered away to another, my soul belongeth solely unto thee!'
grammar_notes: Customary law terminology: 'Man' (bride-price) and 'Kashan' (customary prohibition).
Concessive contrast: 'aphasa khangateili pashitsashu... mangazing nawuisai' (Though body be given, soul is thine).
exercises: Explain the conflict between personal freedom and customary clan authority in Chapter 3.
What traditional gift was paid to seal the betrothal?

chapters.title: The Tragic Farewell & Eternal Union in Spirit
chapters.summary: Shimreishang returns to find Maitonphi has passed away of broken heart; their spirits unite on the mountain crest.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Chapter 4: Shimreishangna kaphung-longkhor kakhorlaga Phadangli ung-kaphung tharan, theilu! Maitonphiwui shimli kathi-laa kakhong theitserie. Maitonphina ningkasham kapei eina awui phasa mathirarlaga Kazingramli valakna! Shimreishangna awui lungkhorli rarlaga lungkashung eina chirpamsai: 'Maitonphi! Na mathida i katha eina ringkapamsara?' Chitharan Shimreishangna awui thàng eina awui lungli kashukserie, kala awui phasa Maitonphiwui ngalemli tuksangie. Ukhrulwui khararchanna hangye: Athum khaniwui mangazing Shirui Kashongli wonkhamathā thada thot pupup ngasomleisaye!
chapters.english_translation: When Shimreishang frantically traversed the gorges and reached Phadang, alas! The haunting strains of the funeral lament echoed from Maitonphi's home. Broken-hearted with grief, she had breathed her last. Collapsing upon her freshly dug stone grave, Shimreishang wept in desperate agony: 'O Maitonphi! How can I endure this earthly life without thee?' Drawing his ancestral dagger, he pierced his own heart and fell beside his beloved. And the ancient legends of the Tangkhul recount: Their spirits transformed into immortal Shirui lilies, blooming together in inseparable embrace upon the mountaintop throughout all eternity.

vocabulary.meaning: funeral song, death lament, requiem dirge

grammar_notes: Funeral lament compound: 'kathi' (death) + 'laa' (song) = dirge.
Immortal transformation narrative motif: physical death giving way to eternal floral rebirth.

lines: Shimreishang kala Maitonphi stands as the undisputed crown jewel of
Tangkhul imaginative prose literature. Comparable in cultural stature to
Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet or Heer Ranjha of Punjab, this epic novel
recounts the star-crossed love of Shimreishang, a valiant youth of the
Zimikwo clan, and Maitonphi, the most graceful maiden of Phadang. It
vividly portrays 18th-century Tangkhul village life, jhum farming
rituals, village festivals, and the tragic conflict between individual
romantic passion and immutable tribal customary codes.

pages.title: The Secret Vow on Shirui Mountain (Shirui Kaphungli Tui-ngashik)
lines: CHAPTER 2: THE SECRET VOW ON SHIRUI MOUNTAIN (SHIRUI KAPHUNGLI TUI-NGASHIK)
Summary: Ascending the mystical heights of Shirui Kashong, the lovers pledge eternal fait...
Chapter 2: Athum khani Shirui Kashong kaphung kashangli thukzat-serie.
Chithuili Shirui Lily won kaphā kachak eina ngasomleisai. Shimreishangna
Maitonphili Shirui Lily akha shitsanglaga awui samli hamsangmi.
Maitonphina mukthi kashik eina hang: 'Shimreishang, ithui shang khaniwui
ngachaili kashan lei; ithui avava-na ithuli ngaror-kashap sara macho?'
Shimreishangna awui khutli huitsanglaga tui-ngashik sakahaisai: 'Ngalei
hi ngapaoritsashu, iwui khangayei nawui vang thot pupup mathimara!'
The two climbed the sacred crest of Mount Shirui, where the unique pink
Shirui Lilies bloomed in virgin purity. Shimreishang plucked a rare
blossom and lovingly placed it in Maitonphi's dark hair. With tears
glistening in her eyes, Maitonphi whispered: 'Shimreishang, an
unyielding clan barrier divides our families; will our parents ever
grant blessing to our union?' Grasping her hand firmly, Shimreishang
swore an inviolable oath: 'Though heaven and earth may vanish away, my
love for thee shall never perish throughout eternity!'

pages.title: Clan Feuds & The Forced Betrothal (Shangwui Kashan kala Kaphankahai)
lines: CHAPTER 3: CLAN FEUDS & THE FORCED BETROTHAL (SHANGWUI KASHAN KALA KAPHANKAHAI)
Summary: Inter-village clan hostilities erupt; Maitonphi's elders betroth her against her...
Chapter 3: Ukhrul kala Phadangwui ngachaili ramkashikhavai tui-ngapom
shokserie. Maitonphiwui avashimna ali Zimikwo shang eina khangayei
sakhavai kakhamrie. Chiwui tharan kashang awungshi akha rarlaga
Maitonphili marriage-wui vang bride-price (Man) mithukserie. Maitonphina
zingsho ngazing kachikhali chirkhangahok eina Shimreishangli
ningkhamathan leisai; kha customary law-wui khongyui kapei eina ana awui
va-vawui tui mathakakhui mashuk-mana. Ana Shimreishangli pao-phungnao
eina kashonmi: 'Iwui aphasa khangateili pashitsashu, iwui mangazing
Bitter clan rivalries erupted between the territories of Ukhrul and
Phadang. Maitonphi's family strictly forbade any association with the
Zimikwo lineage. Soon, an influential chieftain arrived and paid a heavy
customary bride-price for Maitonphi's hand. Maitonphi wept day and night
in inconsolable anguish, yearning for Shimreishang; yet bound by the
iron edict of customary law, she could not disobey her elders. She sent
a secret message: 'Though my physical body be bartered away to another,
my soul belongeth solely unto thee!'
pages.tangkhul_content: Chapter 3: Ukhrul kala Phadangwui ngachaili ramkashikhavai tui-ngapom shokserie. Maitonphiwui avashimna ali Zimikwo shang eina khangayei sakhavai kakhamrie. Chiwui tharan kashang awungshi akha rarlaga Maitonphili marriage-wui vang bride-price (Man) mithukserie. Maitonphina zingsho ngazing kachikhali chirkhangahok eina Shimreishangli ningkhamathan leisai; kha customary law-wui khongyui kapei eina ana awui va-vawui tui mathakakhui mashuk-mana. Ana Shimreishangli pao-phungnao eina kashonmi: 'Iwui aphasa khangateili pashitsashu, iwui mangazing nawuisai!'
